It's so much fun to sit and watch PowerPoint all day long. So I'll do the whole talk in 30 seconds, and then we'll go into more detail. If you're... Let's take a step back. No one ever went into a store to buy a quarter -inch drill bit. What they wanted was a quarter -inch hole, and they were forced to buy the drill bit. No one wants to buy AR or VR or MR. What they want to do is solve a problem, and if the best tool to solve the problem is a digital reality tool, then you'll make sense. The challenge in the marketplace today, and we deal with Fortune 1000, is the hype from Hollywood, the minority report expectation of where and what this magical tool can do, and what wonderful unicorns can jump out of the floor of a gymnasium and dance and do merrily things, doesn't translate to a CEO who's trying to hit numbers the next quarter, the next quarter, the next quarter. And the life expectancy of a CEO of a public company is very short, okay? If you have a kitten, it lasts longer. CMO, it's the half -life. The jokes don't get better, but I'll keep going. You know, CMO has about 36 to 42 -month life expectancy. So the ROI has to be immediate. It has to be massive. It has to be changing. Or it overshadows the risks.

if it's not this amazing miracle, Iron Man going to change the world, Tony Stark, what do we have today? What can we project realistically will be cost -effective to do in the near term next 12 to 18 months, and where does it play? So you don't have to wait for the best headset. You don't even have to wait for any headset. We've actually had augmented reality doing quite well. If you think of broadcast football, we all watch at home, and we know where the first yard line is. We know how much they have to run. We can see all of that. Of it's been overlaid. But what's been missing is the out -of -home experience equivalent of that. If you're in a stadium today or an arena today, you're getting a worse experience than you are at home. So now we have the ability to enhance that out -of -home experience and give you the same level that you've already expected. So nothing new has to be figured out from the UX or UI side of it. All you have to have is a new delivery medium, and those are coming out in the next 12 months. My colleague Alan showed this earlier, which is really, from my standpoint, the psychology of who you're selling to. So right now, there is skepticism on AR and VR in the C -suites across the world. And that skepticism is actually healthy and good because it focuses people not on what a tool can do, not on what the visual range is, not about how many pixels, not how many frames per second per eye, or all the nuance that makes this real. It's we are now at the point where there are actual billion -dollar savings taking place from real -world clients in this space, and we'll go into some of those. So everybody that's focused on changing the Hollywood aspect of it, of what's going to take, that's going to take a much longer cycle because it's facing other issues. And just to put it in perspective, having spent some time on that side of it, less than 10 percent of the U.S. population sets foot in a movie theater each year. This is not going to change that trend. This may bolster aspects. This may create new out -of -home experiences. But that's not where the ROI is. And the first step to ROI is the hardware has to be as mass -produced and as available to the consumer for a very simple reason. When it's at that scale, the consumer will already have the familiarity, just as happened with the PC. Most people did not learn how to use a PC or a smartphone on the job. They were using those in their own lives, and then those tools became part of the workplace. I'm in consulting, so I have to show a graph. Here's two. What they really say, you want, and all these decks are available to everybody so you don't have to try to photograph and then get the small print, is we're talking about a multi -trillion dollar market in a very short period of time, in less than 10 years. So congratulations. You're here. You're focused on a huge growth opportunity. And all you have to do to be successful right now is find one niche that you can deliver ROI, and you will have clients lined up behind you and build those. So we're focused on this because we deal with retailers, manufacturers, virtually every industry that you can think of, and they're facing huge areas. When we break down where those areas are, you're really looking at mobility, e -commerce, B2B, all the areas that you would think, and it's not that there's one area that's going to dominate. This is a tool. This is a fourth transformation. If you think of the PC and the web and mobile, this is of that scale, if not larger. This is bigger than CRM. This is bigger than many of the things. So the places to play right now, safety, both it's mandated in many industries by government, and this is an easier way, an easier solution, and the easiest way to show ROI. Six people died last year. What did that cost you? Okay? When, thank you for the laugh in the back. When things go really wrong in certain industries around safety, the opportunity is there to solve. Design. Most of the tech world believes that everything in the rest of the world is designed in CAD and is this efficient, magnificent process. It isn't. If you knew how much of the world still used clay models to make every part that you see in a car, you would be shocked. So there's huge cost savings in not just reducing cost and waste, but truncating time to respond to consumers' demands and consumer changes. And if you want to talk about an industry that's in the crosshairs right now, the auto industry never had to worry about what you were looking at. You were looking out that window. Okay? Now what will you be doing in a car? Huge fundamental change. What does that do to the interior of the car? What use cases do you now have? How do we transform our lives? Construction. Another issue, another area that technology is pretty much not tapped since, you know, Archimedes and the lever and the pulley. I mean, so huge opportunities to not only visualize and build safer, quicker, and better, but to have more iterations, more input from the client during the process, and less waste during the process, because you can actually walk around your nonexistent building to make sure you're doing it properly. Security. I don't have to tell everybody we're living in an age of heightened security. By the way, no laptops allowed on planes, and you're going to very quickly see an awful lot of goggles selling so people can travel and still do their work. Which brings us to travel. Colocation, the cost of moving people, the distance, the inability in many cases. Huge area, but also the leisure aspect of your dollars are so valuable. You want to experience that location before you go. You want to understand what your choices are. You want to have a feel of that resort, that cruise, that excursion. And retail. Again, if somebody's having their best year, they don't need your help. Retail's having a tough time right now. Now, there's a lot of technologies that are in the favor of retail and will make the smart retailer the choice and destination to have an out -of -home experience that you cannot do just shopping online. So, huge areas to focus on. I'm just going to hit on a few of these, and in 15 minutes, skip. So, training. There's been enough studies. We've been in immersive training for many years now that it's more efficient. But let me give you another thought that we've learned on the training process. For high turnover jobs, training is a sunk cost that keeps them going out the door. You train somebody how to assemble a piece of fast food, and then they go get their next job. You have to train the next person the next. Training is now becoming a heads -up display where you only have to train people to understand that, and the information only gets better and better, and the headset stays when the employee leaves. So, more and more jobs will have the skill set all the way out to the field where if you're repairing a cable system, a phone system, and whatever, you may not know that piece of equipment from 1982 that only Ralph knows, and they have to send and roll a second truck. Now Ralph can stay in a nice air -conditioned office and see what you see and do six or seven different locations. QSRs, you raise the minimum wage. There's only one outcome to that. It is not a better standard of living, and it's not a political statement. It is forcing more automation more quickly. So instead of shadowing another employee for training, you can sit in VR in the corner and learn every aspect and learn the muscle memory of what to do. One fun tip from our designers. We have six design studios with brilliant stuff. Everything that I've seen downstairs and in most places on augmented is adding to the environment. Here's my gift to you today. You can subtract from the environment. So you're putting together the super -duper McJ burger, and in comes the order with no cheese. You go to grab for cheese, and there's no cheese in the cheese bin. You can't put it on the cheeseburger. You can't make the mistake, even though it's really there. This is my favorite example. When you're sitting on a plane, those big metal containers that they slide in, well, there's a bunch of dudes and dudettes whose job is to throw packages in there, and it's a high -turnover job. And if you're doing it for five or more years, you get about 30 % more in. Translate that to metrics. The ones that can't understand 3D -dimensional spatial relationships, you know, they get a job somewhere else. And the overnight shipping company saves a couple billion dollars a year. Safety is a huge area for improvement. It is amazing how many people are injured in certain industries. mean, the number one thing driving self -driving autonomous vehicles that you can't argue against is it saves a million lives. Right? So depending on your industry, depending on the thing, and there's many ways to deal with this. There's the government -mandated way that you can make training happen. You can work with industry. Augmented knowledge. None of us know everything, and none of us know the latest, and none of us can always be up to date. Now you can always have an augmented way to work in your world. This will become not just a killer app for work. This is how we're going to be living our lives. And if you go on the trends, the trends that are driving the next generation of consumers, the era of mass market and everybody getting the same thing is going to the bespoke customized. And this is the way to do that, to start making your design process more fluid and eventually allow the consumer to have input into their product. Hi everyone, so I'm the founder of Immersive Rehab and about eight years ago I had a severe work accident so that basically left me immobile for a very long time. I had no balance for about two years and I had to go through a really long rehab period to get back to the active person that I am today and but going through that rehab period often left me very one isolated, frustrated, demotivated in the way rehab was being done because initially you have quite a lot of access but then suddenly it reduces and you're still not mobile enough to actually do things on your own and that puts a very hard strain. Well it doesn't help your physical mobility but it also puts a heavy strain on your basically your mental health at the same time. So I as a biomedical engineer myself I wanted to use technology to change the way rehab was being done and initially I was just looking into how to make it more engaging and kind of fun also increase access but then when I was looking into other conditions because I only had my own rehab to go on I started looking into strokes, spinal cord injury, thoracic brain injury and I came across really staggering numbers of people leaving especially for upper limb leaving the hospital with about a limit a very limited mobility and on average for stroke for example it's about 15 percent that they gain back with nothing offered after the first six weeks of rehab and so 15 percent is basically you can't do anything with 15 percent of mobility so people lose a lot of the upper limb again and also the lower limb that they've actually gained leading them to complete in dependent state again and same goes for spinal cord injury and so on and so also the long waiting times were really are a really big issue because a lot of the for example I work with Royal London Hospital and they have waiting times at the complex spine unit that go up to nine months depending on to be transferred from the hospital unit into a rehab facility for example which leaves people with one they lose a big window of recovery and also the the people there they get really demotivated depressed and worse and then to get out of it it's very hard so um so yeah I started looking into how can we change that and so when looking into um mechanisms to actually help people gain more that mobility back um I came across this concept which is basically neuroplasticity and everybody I don't know if you're aware of neuroplasticity but everybody uses it when you learn something new when you didn't know how to brush your teeth you basically when you were learning it you use a toothbrush and you basically use it and now it's a natural thing you know how to do it it's like opening doors riding a bike and new things so currently people often physios they they don't ask patients anymore to engage with objects because they get really frustrated because they don't have strength fine motor skills so they don't want to do the exercises anymore they tune out and so now they just ask do this movement 20 times this movement 20 times but when you want to link it to a movement or opening something it actually your brain does not register if you do this specific movement you actually want to link it to brushing your teeth opening a door and so on and so with this concept of neuroplasticity you want to kind of reinstate the connection between your brain that has been damaged with your motion and currently the tools that physios use are too limited they because they don't use objects and they don't have visual stimulation tools so with vr we can actually allow people to engage with objects where in the physical world they can't so that is um basically what is what immersive rehab is about is to reinstate that connection and help people gain more of that mobility back so if you just compare it currently with how current rehab is being done there's really lack of compliance really long waiting times um fine motor skill training and upper limb training is so that mostly occupational therapists too physiotherapists as well it's it's harder in a way to help people advance it takes longer often than than other types of more general physiotherapies so that often and also the tools that they have are limited so that that is why then when you look at vr and the options that vr has to for example also do like bilateral movements in the physical world it would often be impossible to do this movement but in the virtual world you could actually train it with a virtual object that has no weight but people think that they're moving this ball around the box around and so on so it's really tricking your brain as well um and yeah quicker access is a really big thing so um so this is our platform it's it's uh one of one of the kind of physiotherapy exercises that is based on the grasping method so people like reach grab put and so instead of doing 20 times the same movement um moving the arm to the right and so we just mix everything up and the goal is to build towers against a certain time within a specific time so this is very much um adapted to stroke patients and spinal cord injury patients or patients with upper limb disabilities because of the way the the movements are being done the ergonomics the time we have different we can do it sitting standing we have different um difficulties as you can see here um so depending on and you see so this is mia she's a stroke patient in a hospital in north london and you see her she's moving her feet and she actually has a very severe balance issue because of her stroke and yeah so that was a very um um important kind of uh collaboration with them to to actually co -design the games that are suitable for those type of patients um another patient that i've worked with is david smith he's a paralympic athlete so he was a gold medalist in 2012 for great britain in rowing uh for the paralympics but he's also he's also been a spinal cord injury patient three times because of the spinal tumor in his neck so he's paralyzed from the waist down and upper limb affected like a stroke and he was using visual stimulation on a constant basis like on a daily basis and and for athletes it's been really special to work with them in a sense marginal gains are everything so zero one percent gain it's that is a gain and and that has been really incredible and so so he was walking again all three times almost after eight weeks because of like visual stimulation imagining i can move my feet and really working on those on their neurological rehabilitation as well so um so yeah just going um over like two case studies as well that i've worked with um with a a young man in his 20s that had traumatic brain injury and spinal cord injury um and because of his cognitive issues as well he was not engaged so after one minute he tunes out he doesn't want to do it and basically because of that reason he doesn't advance so he's still very much um in kind of uh his mobility hasn't really improved much so within the vr rehab um exercises um he his engagement increases increased and obviously there's a novelty aspect as well i completely realized that but he was in it for 10 minutes with severe cognitive issues and he wanted to do it over again he was very focused and that was very interesting to see for the occupational therapist she was like what is happening so that was that was really interesting and then the the second man that i worked with was a man in a 60 60s just had a stroke um with one side affected and he he was coming in and he was like i don't want to really do this and but then when he once he was in it he was very engaged as well then the other interesting thing was outside of vr when people were asking to move when the physio would ask can you move your arm uh for example that far to the right and then the patient would say no i i can't so this is kind of my limits um and and yeah when you have something injured or something you kind of want to protect your injury even though you can actually move for that but in vr so when he was doing the block building game he was just building the towers and he was reaching a lot further in a very safe way not really over straining or anything so that was really interesting as well and kind of taking away limitation and also being in a world that is not a clinical environment um so and they're very independent so they basically do every as much possible they determine their own kind of difficulties and exercises in a way uh so Hi, my name is Dad Anson. I'm founder and president of Brick Simple, a studio with offices in Boston, Philadelphia, and San Francisco. And what I wanted to share today was really we talked so much about augmented reality and really talking about creating these experiences that really feel different and take advantage of the features of augmented reality headsets. I mean, often from a user experience perspective, we were spoiled by design aspects of the web just translating the mobile devices as glass rectangles, touchscreens instead of pointers. And really when you're designing for AR, it helps to think, no, I hate to use the think differently, but you do want to think differently. So first I just want to talk about the HoloLens. I mean, the HoloLens is this device, you know, you can call it a Concord moment. We call it the Apple II of wearable AR, see -through AR. It has, to its credit, this wonderful self -contained design. It integrates all these features which were not science fiction long ago. The fact that it works as a complete device, has wonderful spatial tracking, makes it truly remarkable. We all kind of accept its faults, but we adore the future that it promises. And as you see here, and you see the person there, it also has it awkward. Everyone's seen the awkward little pinch -click gesture, telltale sign of HoloLens fatigue. But it really did introduce all of this in one working package for the first time. As John mentioned, we did a lot of work with Google Glass. We've done work with other augmented reality devices. We've seen many come and go over the past decade. But when we saw HoloLens, this was a device that could realize really, truly cool experiences. So I have here, you see Matt and our team of MIT, oddly enough. And you see here CPR being performed as seen through the HoloLens. This is an award -winning experience that we developed working with the University of Pennsylvania Center for Resuscitation Science. And a spun -out entity called Emerge Labs, founded by Marion Leary. And what we were able to do is give direct feedback to how your CPR is being performed on a mannequin. We tie in live data through the Internet of Things. Tie in live data so that you can see what's happening. So the person who's performing CPR can get immediate feedback. And then also someone who's coaching or other students can see what's happening when you're performing CPR. And as you see circulation happening there, if you don't perform CPR effectively, you will eventually see that brain go gray. It's very sad. But it does give you that feedback. And what we wanted to do when we created this experience is we wanted something that has no menus, no buttons. I'm not... I always felt with glass. The moment I touched side of my head, we failed from a design perspective. And whenever I'm doing this, I feel like we failed. So we wanted to have something that you simply put on, tracks to the mannequin and makes it all work. And doing an experience like this really does push and test the metal of the augmented reality experience of developing. But one of the things you'll notice with this is how tightly that circulatory system model tracks to the actual mannequin. And when folks talk about tracking and they show off their tracking, it's one thing to have planets floating in space. It's quite another to have it mapped to an object in the real world. What I also love about this kind of approach using real world objects is the haptics problem is solved. You have a real physical reaction and feedback to what you're doing. So I take an experience like this, take a time like this, what is it like to bring something like this to other platforms? So here we have the meta and we're big fans of meta. Meta is interesting in that it has a wider field of view of the HoloLens. But it also has hand tracking. You can actually go reach out and grab things and not just pinch things like pixie dust. You can really go out there and reach. It is a tethered device. It's not self -contained. But having been a fan of meta and watching it evolve, they're shipping a real product you can put on your head right now. So taking an experience from the HoloLens and trying to miss how well do we make that work on a meta? How well can that work? So if we look at this here, I'm going to click a little harder. So here we see two of our guys. And one of things you'll notice is that the meta has this advantage of having all this horsepower of the attached PC. But its spatial tracking isn't super 100 % great yet. If you compare that to where we were on the HoloLens where the circulatory system was clearly coupled and anchored in the mannequin, here as you move around, it plays a little catch -up in the meta. And I also share everything we're showing here. This is done shot through the devices in this case. This is through the feed of the meta, the HoloLens as well, and the others. I like that real stuff versus rendered because you can see what's actually going on. You can also see here, as you see the cable stretched across, is that Tyler is moving along. He's tethered to a PC to do this. Advantage, course, of this platform is that it is, you know, it's lower cost than the HoloLens. You can do more things at scale. And it does have a lot of strengths, but this kind of movement for this kind of application, particularly in healthcare, part of the challenge of working on it with the meta device for healthcare applications. And they're making improvements to tracking. We're seeing improvements. But to really make these things work well, you have to consider the hardware capabilities to have that kind of immersive experience.

[None]
So

[SPEAKER_00]
we'll take a step back from those see -through wearables. One of the great things that happened in AR was Apple including ARKit. That was so important because prior to that, you had to go and, you know, you paid a license of some kind to embed this functionality in your application. It didn't come built in for free. It wasn't necessarily optimized for the hardware. And through Apple's acquire, by Apple acquiring Matayo, they were really able to bring something that was quite powerful and effective. And one of the things we love about this platform is the slam tracking that it has is amazingly good for a device that has no special sensors in it whatsoever. Tracks very well. It's fantastic in that way. We look at applications. currently using this in orthopedics because you can provide that seamless kind of experience. Unfortunately, you're still holding that glass rectangle. You're still holding this rectangle which compromises the immersiveness of it. Doesn't make it seem as seamless. When we had that HoloLens on our head, it felt like magic. We look down and we can see into that body below us and interact with it. That's one of the reasons why we really like this device. First thing this morning for the folks who managed to see it, Matayo Hue showed HoloKit. And we've been big fans of HoloKit because the devices I've shown here when we're talking, the HoloLens, it's $3,000 and up. You're looking at a meta, it's $1,000 plus hardware to make it work and go. With the Apple stuff is great with the $1,000 phone. What we love about HoloKit is this way to democratize access these experiences. And when you think about something like training someone in CPR, if I have a room full of people, putting a HoloLens on each of their heads is not cost effective. But I can have one HoloLens and then have others share in that experience using this device. We don't get any, I use device in almost quotes, it's cardboard. But here we're not using any special sensors like the meta or the HoloLens. We're not, all we're doing is making use of the camera and the self -contained features of the phone to make it work. And it can work quite well. So we can take that and someone can hold it, looks a little bit like a periscope. But we actually do get very good tracking. In this case we use the mannequin to, the mannequin we have a 3D model, we actually track to the model of the mannequin. It's stable, this is a build, receive, work in progress. But we actually can provide bystanders and folks access to this kind of see -through AR. And that's the part that I've seen, I've seen evolve with our involvement in augmented reality over the past decade, is that the accessibility of these kind of experiences, things that we just kind of had fancifully on the whiteboard and on the to -do list, that we can make that happen and work. And when you take a device like HoloKit, which you can order on Amazon for $30, you're talking a two -order magnitude difference in price. And a great increase in terms of accessibility. Now granted there are limitations, but we also created this as something that you're not clicking on menus, you're not relying on someone tapping in the air, that what you do is simply look down and be engaged. And healthcare use cases makes a lot of sense, education, industry, to give that kind of quick view and look. So as we're thinking about experiences, mean sometimes this hardware, and I think there's a great comment on the panel earlier, this hardware is like printers. know, two years from now at AR in action we're going to be talking about some whiz -bang new hardware and there will be a collection of devices that are in that HoloLens class of experience. But devices like HoloKit, Meta, really allow us to explore and build these experiences now. And I'm very excited about that being in this space. I am obviously a big old nerd. But for us, we really see a huge opportunity in work that we've done here in healthcare, work that we've done in industry, where these enterprise applications are here now and really enabled by these technologies. So I just want to thank everyone for the opportunity to present some of these pieces. We do have a table over in the demo area if you'd like to check it out. My contact information is here. I'm happy to speak and answer questions beyond the presentation. Thank you very much.
sources.title: Designing Context Driven Augmented Reality Experiences for Healthcare | Det Ansinn | ARIA

Good afternoon everyone. This is the most disconcerting thing for a speaker, is when you get up and everybody's leaving. It's like you've seen all the pretty faces in AR and VR. Can

[None]
guys hear me?

[SPEAKER_00]
And now you're going. And I'm the last person between you and the tea break, or the beer break if you're Australian like me. So I get that. There's another acknowledgement I need to make. I'm new at AWE. This is my first time here. Who else is new at AWE? Yep, excellent. I've been seeing all the speakers and they all start something like this. I'm a PhD in AR and VR. I've been working for 23 years in the industry and I'm 14 years old. And we've got 17,000 clients and I'm going to show you just two of the use cases today. And they're the same use cases from presentation to presentation. There we go. go with this one. Hey! That's much better. And so no use cases at all in my presentation. No use cases. I haven't been in AR, VR for 23 years. I do not have a PhD. In fact, I've spent the vast bulk of my career, yes I do have a white beard, in corporate life. My most previous role was Chief Technologist for Innovation at Hewlett Packard Enterprise across Asia Pacific Japan. So I have been working with big clients around emerging technologies and AR and VR was the one that I chose to follow when I left corporate world. So lastly, what I'd like to say is I'd like to give you some tips and tricks. We've seen a lot of what. Here's what, right? We've even had Kirim pose a really good question. Is AR too expensive for the enterprise because nobody's buying it? If it's so great, why is nobody buying it? I'd like to answer that question with a third option. He gave two options. But I agree with his second option as well. But what I do want to do in the next 15 or so minutes is leave you with a bit of a how. Right? Here's how I approach enterprises. So the business reality of virtual reality trips off the tongue. The business reality of augmented, mixed, blended, holographic and virtual reality doesn't trip off the tongue. So when I say virtual reality, I'm basically talking about all of those. And I just want to make sure I look. Push the big green button. So three years ago, five years ago, this. Whoa. Here we go back. Five years ago, we didn't expect to see this in our world. And yet here it is. As I think it's Jim Schell said in his presentation, you know, the 10 year old says, what was it like to live in the world of ignorance? Right? And we just have information at our fingertips. I took a trip. I rented a motorbike on Saturday. And I rode up through Northern California. And I had augmented reality in the headset of my motorbike helmet. Audio augmented reality of Google telling me exactly where I needed to go. Right? And we just, it's ubiquitous. But this isn't really scalable. No, nobody, no businesses want to see this. In fact, businesses when they see this go, is that like a game? Is that like Pokemon Go? I don't want all my workers to be looking at their phones, not at their work. I guess unless the phones are their work. I guess This slide is either dystopia, if you're like everybody else in the world, or utopia if you're a marketing expert. Or Japanese. Sorry, I don't mean to be dismissive. But this is kind of one of the future views, right? That we get to see all this augmented reality in our line of sight throughout the day. Nobody really wants to look like this, do they? Like even factory workers. just heard how factory workers are really happy about using technology for blue collar workers now, rather than just for white collar workers. But I rather suspect that most factory workers don't want to look like that. They probably don't want to wear a HoloLens. I have a HoloLens. I use it to demonstrate to my clients all the time. I take it off their heads after about 45 seconds, because that's about the point at which you start really feeling the weight of the HoloLens. 45 minutes is a stretch. I've played the game Fragments. And it's a four hour game. And I played it in like one hour stretches over four different stretches, right? It's just that the HoloLens is, it's fantastic technology. It's just not there yet for an enterprise use. And then of course, we saw this slide yesterday. Tom had this slide as well, Tom Emrick. And you know, this is pretty much what most executives think of virtual reality. Like you go and talk to them about how virtual reality can save them money. And they just envision their workplace turning into this. Ready player one. Okay, so why then do we think there is a business reality for virtual reality? And that's really because business drivers can be summed up in three things. Businesses want to increase growth. And that exhibits as profit, revenue, market share, right? Businesses want to grow. That's their business driver. Another business driver is businesses want to reduce costs. They want to become more efficient, more productive, save money, reduce costs for their clients. And then the third thing is, and we've seen a lot of this recently with BP and Enron and a whole bunch of other companies, is they have to comply. Right? If you are going to sell AR into the medical industry, good luck. Because, you know, you've got HIPAA and you've got health and safety and you've got all sorts of FDA and federal requirements around compliance. Right? And the truth is that, of course, VR can, or VR and AR can absolutely help you achieve one or preferably more of those things. So here's the first how. When you're speaking to executives about a solution, speak to executives about their business drivers. Have a look at their annual reports. What are they going to do? Are they going to grow? And how are they going to grow? Are they going to grow organically? Are they going to grow strategically? Are they going to buy, grow through acquisitions and mergers? Are they going to shrink in one geography and grow in another geography? Do they want to grow in a different demography? Right? Think about their business strategy around growth. Think about their business strategy around saving costs, becoming more productive. Because that's the language that they speak. Talk to them about compliance. Compliance to security, to safety regulations, to regulatory compliance around financial industry, etc. Okay. We saw a similar slide to this yesterday. Yesterday, and this basically is looking at the value chain and saying, where can AR and VR help you achieve these goals or goals for these drivers across your value chain? And I don't need to go into that anymore. And I need to save time. So I'm going to go forward. But I'm going to let you have your beer earlier. Or if you're not Australian, your cup of tea. And if you're American, your coffee. Okay. So why AR and VR? Here's another tip. When we speak to executives, take them to where they're at. Don't talk about this cool technology, but talk to them about where are you at. So I love to use this example. I did a bunch of sailing in Antigua back in the early 90s. And whether you're a sailor or not, if you look at that picture, you will automatically start noticing things. Like, all the yachts face the same direction. What does that tell you? Well, there's probably some kind of tide or wind or current pushing all the, you know, dragging the yachts on their anchors in the same direction. And you get that intuitively because your mind is spatial. And so now you have an insight even if you're a non -domain expert. So where in the business value chain will an insight for a non -domain expert help them grow, save, or comply? Right? If you talk to executives in that language, they get it. Right? These guys aren't stupid. They're just not very keen on technology like we are. Okay. The second one is, what about your domain experts? Can you accelerate the information from them? We were talking to a large federal organization that collects revenue from every citizen and business in our country. And we were talking about doing big data visualization. And we were saying, you know, you could see 30 years of transactions and you could overlay it in demography and geography and everything else. And that will help you with your strategy and your policies. And they went, you know, all we want to see is tax returns in real time overlaid on a map that we can drill into by postcode and then compare it to last year. That's all. Right? Really, really simple. But that will save us three weeks of work for the tax commissioner every time he goes to see the minister. Right? So there's three weeks of preparation for a monthly meeting that involves hundreds of people and hundreds of strategists. And if you could just see that information in 3D and overlay just those two dimensions, that would save all that money. Right? So think about accelerating insights for non -domain experts. Oh, and for domain experts. And then, of course, what about new insights for domain experts? If you're trying to build a building, you've probably got some engineer and architect or an architect drawing up blueprints and an engineer building the building on blueprints. And you've got some project manager and construction worker working on a project plan. Right? And the construction worker or the project manager can't see the gates that are going to be blocked during the scale of the build. And the guys working on the blueprints don't understand the timeline of the build. Right? So by putting them together in 3D in VR, you can actually start to see where production overruns might happen. Or you can start to see where you need to change your logistics onto the site. So VR can actually give domain experts new insights that they wouldn't have seen already. It can give non -domain experts insights that they wouldn't get, obviously. And it can accelerate insights for domain experts. Okay. So how then do we talk to... Oh, so yeah. So here's where we are today. We saw a similar slide to this in Karim's presentation. So this is what everybody in the business is doing at the moment. They're looking at a 2D screen. They might not be looking so happy. And this is where we want to get to tomorrow. Of course, I should have used the Jarvis picture, but there you go. And to go from here to here, and here's the third answer to Karim's question. I believe that a lot of reasons that people aren't using AR at the moment or buying AR is because of this. They're simply not aware. They're not aware of how our spatial minds and the accessibility... ...one minute. You're joking. You must have cut off five minutes of my talk. Okay. So I'm gonna swizz through this. So the words in orange are the challenges that you have across that life cycle. And the challenges that you have for us solution providers is those are the opportunities. This is where we can help, right? We can provide capable talent. You can showcase... Have a showcase environment, et cetera. All right. And these are the two domains that you do this in. Obviously, the development domain and... Or the design and development domain. And then the training and education domain. Okay. And moving on very quickly then. So this is what my business is doing. We're providing AR, VR training as a service, innovation as a service. And we're actually starting with AR and VR services to give examples to executives on how they can achieve the adjacent possible. But ultimately, as per Karim and Andreas' presentation, you've got to get this to Software Factory. You can't do a bespoke solution for every executive problem, for every business or enterprise problem. So a couple of tools then to help with that Software Factory. Here's one that I use all the time. The first thing that people talk about is what's the financial attractiveness, right? What's the investment? What's the return? And different companies use different markers. So some companies might use internal rate of return. Some companies might use TCO, total cost of ownership. Some might use return on investment. It doesn't really matter. My chart will give them whatever criteria they want to use. Then we look at a Y axis of strategic value. So how does it align to your market priorities, to your business strategy? How does the solution, how technology efficient is it? So does it integrate easily? Has it been done before? How long does it take to deploy, et cetera? And then we look at a fourth index, which is business and technical risk. And then we plot all of the ideas, all of the solutions that we've been speaking to them about through that program. And very, very easily for an executive in their language, they can look at the four or five or six innovations that we've come up with around AR and VR and go, okay, we probably, whoops. We probably want to go with, you know, that one. It's really aligned to our strategy. It's fairly risky, but it's within our risk plan. And it's really efficient from a technology perspective. And then maybe that'll be solution number two and that'll be solution number three, et cetera. Okay. All right. It's

[None]
online, so I can't help you with it at the moment.

[SPEAKER_00]
Thanks, Google. This is the last slide. I do want to show this very quickly. I'm sorry I'm out of time. This one basically takes away any of the confusion from a solution definition problem, right? So if you think about all the things that AR and VR can give you, so you need to be able to access it. How many people need to be able to access the solution? How mobile do they need to be? How much do they need to collaborate with other people? How are they going to control the solution? How immersed do they need to be? What agency do they need to have? So how much interactivity? What about alterity? Do you want to give them a different type of experience? And then what are you going to analyze, right? And then there's another index, which is how much does it need to integrate with your current software? And then what that allows you to do is really just go, you know, let's just do a pattern. And we can see that, you know, once we've defined the problem, how we want to solve the problem, it'll tell us that it's a Samsung Gear VR 360 video with a CGI overlay, right? So that can then just, again, this is coming back to the software factory, where you can just very, very quickly even self -diagnose or self -design at least the input to the conversation about the solution for the enterprise. Okay, that is it. I am definitely over time. You guys definitely need a beer. Thank you very much for your attention. Really enjoyed your time. And there is at least one question over there.

[SPEAKER_01]
So the question to repeat it is what industries that Roger's company has been focused on so far?

you think partnering with a range of technology providers is key?

One of the questions for the panel was, how do you find the best AR and designer? There we go. There it is. Thanks very much. How do you find these capabilities? Thank you, John. Maybe a little bit of Han Solo mixed in, . So, amazing range of topics here at AR is intersecting with. And I hope I can add a little bit to the discussion with a presentation on simulating the future of AR, which so many of us are doing. So, I co -direct what is known as the 4Is lab at UC Santa Barbara. The 4Is stands for Imaging Interaction and Innovative Interfaces. But I want to start with a nod to Steve, because it was an absolute privilege for me to join his group in the mid -1990s and be part of a team that was working on the first outdoor mobile augmented reality system. And so, we did something like this. The building that you see there is what covered Columbia's grounds before Columbia moved there. And fittingly, it is the Bloomingdale Asylum for the insane, which causes people to say that things do not change in history. And this is what we looked like in 1997, 1998 in this case. And, yeah, people were calling out Ghostbusters after us. And come to think of it, backpacks for augmented reality or virtual reality and Ghostbusters, sounds very much like 2016. So, maybe just a glitch in the matrix. We fast forward to, or back from 2016 to 2007. I started at UC Santa Barbara in 2003. And in 2007, one of our projects was very much against all this equipment. We used computer vision to bootstrap and to track an admittedly fairly small space. So, we used the outstretched hand as a marker and interface element to grab virtual objects and populate a virtual desktop that kind of made your physical desktop a little bit more interesting. And so, this is part of the journey of going on and simulating AR because AR in its perfection is not attainable and will not be maybe ever. It depends on your definition of perfection. And in our case, around that time, this was the limited workspace that was covered, just a desktop. And there was a SLAM system that actually could build this model about this fairly small space over time. But it had its definite constraints. So, in 2012, then, we went outdoors trying to cut a few more tethers and getting a little bit wider in the area. And there you have the Star Trek reference. I don't think that John knew that. We would actually bring some content in here. So, this is not a SLAM system. In 2012, my PhD student, John Ventura, here in the picture, actually came up with a very clever, very quick way of building a point cloud off, of any large -scale outdoor environment by just walking through it with an omnidirectional camera. And then using the structure from motion data cloud that you got from that to track against from just an iPad. So, a 2012 iPad in this case. And so, that worked fairly well, as long as you have nice facades to look at and not empty space or wavy shrubbery or whatever other things could get this tracking system to fail. And so, this is just another example of shifting boundaries. We have better systems now. And the HoloLens is clearly currently commercially, in terms of commercially available systems, one of the most impressive stand -alone tracking systems. So, last year, we did this with a HoloLens. We annotated objects from afar with simple gestures. And then, so, if you, courtesy of the mapping that the HoloLens does, so the object is actually has a representation in polygons. And so, from a distance, you can actually place annotations that live exactly at the object. And so, we built a few gesture recognition systems in there so that you could have some gestures to annotate the space. But as we all know who have used the HoloLens, also that is not perfect. So, when I borrow an example from our book, Dieter Schmarstig and I finished a book last year on augmented reality, principles and practice. And just to show what could happen in a scenario like this, where you would want augmented reality in a surgery situation. If you have a system that doesn't augment your entire field of view, you would get something like this, where the overlay field of view is actually fairly small. And it happens to be fairly small for the HoloLens at the moment. So, the quest continues with, like, basically, this is another step in just simulating the perfect AR. And wouldn't it be nice if we could really simulate an infinite field of view, or a human field of view, for augmented reality? And so, since about 2009, this is something that we thought about a little bit more organized in an organized fashion in my lab. So, this is work with Doug Bauman from Virginia Tech as well. And we use a system, virtual reality system, which currently is fairly advanced, the virtual reality systems, in terms of immersion. So, their realism rises faster at the moment than augmented reality in terms of different immersion factors like field of view, resolution, and so on. And if you have a high immersion virtual reality system, which could be a head -worn system, or it could be a cave -like system. At UC Santa Barbara, we have a large -scale immersive spherical system, the Allosphere, which I will mention and show you in a few minutes. If you have such a high fidelity virtual reality system, you can actually simulate other systems in the mixed reality spectrum of a lower fidelity. And, of course, the immersion axis is not one single axis. It would actually be split up in many, many dimensions. But I think the picture gives the overview. So, what do I mean by simulating augmented reality and virtual reality? Well, so, we ran a few validation studies. So, as a famous, one of the famous early experiments in AR by Steve Ellis, where a torus was kind of guided over a virtual wire, in a real space. And so, this is what it would look like to simulate that, a little bit clumsily admittedly, in virtual reality. And by doing so and getting the same result for that study, we have one data point that says doing this is actually worthwhile. Because if it were worthwhile for a large area of applications, then you could actually now run controlled user studies of very new, new and otherwise not possible, AR research questions. And so, we ran a few more validation and immersion studies on this concept. This one here deals with trying to assess the impact of the fidelity of the real world backdrop. So, in the simulated augmented reality, you need a representation of the real world. And you do this in virtual reality. So, it doesn't make a difference if this real world is actually fairly realistic across many dimensions in terms of polygon count, lighting, texture, and so on and so forth. And so, we built different accuracy, different realism models of the same physical scene, as you can see here. And then ran a user study with a particular test in augmented reality, both in the real world and then in virtual reality in this different fidelity environments. And the outcome was that the main results, again, stayed stable. There were some differences, and especially some differences, and this is why I put the picture up here in the bottom, that deal with high dynamic range lighting, for example, that is very hard to replicate in the virtual reality system that we used for this, which was for this very study, a head -1 display, before head -1 displays became a little bit better. So, but in general, it gave us confidence that the approach actually is interesting and very worthwhile. So, instead of a head -1 display, you can actually run such studies also in an immersive, surround -1 display. This is the allosphere. So, this is a three -story high spherical display, about 10, 11 meters in diameter. It's not exactly spherical. It's two hemispheres pushed apart, so that you don't have an acoustic sweet spot in the middle. But a bridge goes right through it. It's a little bit like Cerebro. The brain interfaces come later. We had access through Tom DeFanti to this great, beautiful panorama, stereo panorama of the Luxor Temple in Egypt. Because, again, I'm simulating a head -worn display, but everything is projected onto the panoramic backdrop of this large -scale display. And so, with this, we can run studies and figure out what field of view actually lets people perform best in the task of finding my information in such a space. And it turns out that you need at least 60 to 80 degrees in order to not have a big drop -off in performance. And I invite people to come and experience this, because even wider field of views are actually something that we not commonly think about. So, down the road, we run many controlled studies on the influence of a variety of immersion factors. Latency, field of regard, which you see in an example here on the right, slightly different from field of view. Scene realism. Many compromises are still being struck with our simulation environment. It's not reality. And the search does go on. But I'm specifically interested in this question of a wide field of view. If an architect is standing in front of a building in the space that it will be constructed, then they should see in the entire field of view the building filling and coming up in front of them. Right? And they should even be able to step inside of the building and actually look out the window and see the physical reality through the window. But if they're inside, they see all the details of that architectural design. So it's a mixture of virtual reality and augmented reality. And in fact, I would say in the limit, virtual reality and augmented reality do converge. I mean, in the latest time when we have real -time realistic scene reconstruction and rendering of the world in front of us and can use that to create new experiences. And that would really reap the benefit of both. And with that, I thank the researchers that actually did this work in my lab and our sponsors. Thank you very much.

But anyways hi, I'm excited to be here. Hi. I'm Sarah Downey. I'm a principal at Accomplice which is an early stage VC firm here in Boston. We used to be called Atlas Venture. We split in half. They do life science. We do tech. So my background is I was a lawyer. Didn't want to practice. Worked at a couple startups. Now I'm investing specifically in AR and VR. But one thing that I think qualifies me to talk on this stuff perhaps more than any of that stuff is that I'm a huge sci -fi and video game person. So yeah, a lot of recognition from you out here. And that's definitely a common thread that I see everywhere. Like we've wanted this stuff to be reality for a long time and now we're at that inflection point where it's actually becoming reality. So I don't know about all of you but I feel really lucky to be alive right now. I think that this is the most exciting time for humanity and we're in it. So with this, you know, everyone in this room is here because we believe that AR is going to be big and we're all excited about it. And I wanted to compile a list of some of what I think is most exciting about that. And I did this in an article for Upload VR where I contribute. I tried to list as many discrete interesting things by category as I could. Some of these might be novel to you and some of them won't. But I think often we encounter people who say, I don't really get this AR thing. I don't know why it's big. And so I'm trying to give enough use cases that you can go and tell those people like, hey, I heard about this today. And this will affect you or your job or your life in some way. And I have to cut this down massively for this talk. But if you want to check out the whole thing, that's the URL. Another big thing is that in venture, we have to predict the future. And we are too early sometimes, which is bad because people aren't ready to adopt a product and things don't really work out. It's also bad if we're too late because there's too many competitors and things aren't really that exciting once it's been done before. So for each of these use cases, I'm going to talk a little bit about a near term thing, which might be the next couple of years, and a long term thing, which might be 10, 15, 20 plus years out. In productivity, one of the most interesting things, I think, is the shift in UI, UX from what we currently do, which is mostly touch and typing, to brain computer interfaces, to voice, eye tracking, to these new forms of gestures and things like you already see in the HoloLens, the bloom gestures and the point. And then long term, several of speakers have mentioned this today, but the fact that you can have a high res display anywhere is going to get rid of screens. It's going to get rid of TVs. It's going to get rid of like these clunky monitors that we plop ourselves in front of. We're going to be able to do this anywhere at any time. I also like the idea of using facial recognition and detection to, in real time, scan a person's face, pull up this whole digital footprint of them, all of your past interactions, what they tweeted, what they're doing on LinkedIn, is kind of scary from a privacy perspective. But it also empowers all of us to kind of have that superpower to be the person that remembers every interaction that you've ever had with anybody, and what their kids are doing, what they do, and remember, you know, why you're going into a meeting and what the context was. In psychology, have some things that you've already been talked about today, but EQ training, right? AR can allow you to analyze people. Are they interested in what you're saying at that very moment? Are they smiling? Are they happy with their sentiment? Have you been telling a joke for too long? Should you maybe back off? You know, there's special application for the autistic community with applications like these. And then long term, empathy training. AR and VR can put us literally in each other's bodies. So if you want to be in somebody else's shoes, these types of technologies can put you there. And already there's research on how impactful this can be for understanding each other. There's a lot in transportation. I think this is one of the easiest things to wrap your head around when it comes to AR, because, again, near term, you're taking this phone and looking down, especially when you're driving, which can be dangerous, right? And just simply moving that up in a headset so that you're looking at the road and you're seeing these directions transposed on top of your field of view. So first of all, that's going to be a lot better in terms of safety. And then longer term, you're going to have navigation inside of places like malls, which pulled into real -time inventory management could show you, you know, here's all the black leather jackets in this mall and you can go there. So that's going to be super useful. We've heard a lot about education today. And this, I think, is one of the biggest areas with interesting use cases. But near term, we can look at things like a physical book or even an e -book and have AR pop -outs. We can have 3D visualizations of charts. We can have videos. We can define words. Like, you know, the Kindle is already a very early example of this where you can look something up in the dictionary if you don't get it. But long term, the fact that teachers and educators can create very personalized content that reacts to you, you know, can slow down a course if you're not comprehending, can speed it up for somebody who's quicker, can do real -time quizzes. Very interesting, in my opinion. Law enforcement and legal has a lot of implications, some of which, again, are scary from a privacy perspective, but there's always this tension between privacy and liberty, right? So short term, the ability to scan faces in crowds and be able to search for suspects. And also using people's phones or, in the future, people's headsets to sort of do crowd -sourced manhunts. And longer term, again, I'm referencing things that have been brought up today, which today has been amazing in my opinion, so many cool things. But one of those is that AR can detect micro -expressions. So all of us, when we're lying, generally we all kind of have these micro -expressions that betray us and show that we might not be telling the truth. So you can imagine the implications for things like jury selection, where you might want to tell a little fib to get out of that, or negotiation, you would have to be much more straightforward, or even trials. You know, if somebody's on the stand, will that be the kind of evidence that we'd be able to use? And crime scene recreation. There's already some work with this in VR, but you can imagine in AR, capturing reality at the scene of a crime, and then showing that to a prosecutor, to a jury in the future. You know, being able to really put yourself in the shoes of a person at the scene of a crime, and gauge, you know, could I actually see a bullet from this standpoint? Could I actually identify a person from this far away? Some of my favorite use cases are in accessibility, because AR can really give us senses that we don't have, and give us superpowers to the ones that we do. So some of the short -term applications are things like magnifying text, real -time language translation, but the longer term for the visually impaired includes applications like translating objects to audio. So we were talking in the last, the last guy, Samson, was talking about computer vision. So, you know, the ability for your AR headset or device to pick up all the objects in the world around you, and give that to a visually impaired person through their audio channel, is life -changing for those individuals. Or similarly, for hearing impaired people, getting like a real -time closed caption feed of what sounds, and what things are happening to them. Like, I'm getting on a plane right after this, and you know, when the pilot makes an announcement, that's the thing that, you know, we kind of take for granted that we can all hear that, but a hearing impaired person with this kind of headset in the future could either see a American Sign Language person, sort of like as an inset box, or just have the closed captioning on the bottom. And, you know, there's companies working on both of these things right now. We heard a lot about medical today, so I'll make this one brief, but the ability to get a second pair of eyes, a second opinion on something that a doctor is seeing right then is happening today. And then long -term, to be able to go in remotely with robotics, and complete a surgery that really scales somebody who's a specialist in a medical field, who might be limited by travel, in order to make that person more accessible. There's been a lot of developments in AR in the military. It's been one of the places with the most innovation in the past, and some of the best technology that we've seen that actually has a history in the military. So, today we're already seeing enhanced pilot heads -up displays to track, to better track targets, for navigation and aim. But then, one of my favorite future applications is, this comes from the gaming world, but to do an exaggerated display around friendlies and civilians, with like a green aura, and enemies with red, to minimize accidental casualties. I'm kind of intentionally minimizing shopping and advertising, because I think there's, we've all heard a lot about that as applied to AR, but I do think it's interesting in the kind of shorter term, next couple of years, to imagine a smart grocery store trip with your AR glasses, where you know, you check things off of a list, and maybe you have a navigation through the grocery store that shows you the best path to get the items that you need, and you hit the, you know, the freezer last, so your things don't melt. And then long -term, let's say you walk by somebody on the street, and they have a cool pair of shoes, right? This is in development, but to my knowledge, doesn't exist yet. You would be able to look at that person, kind of flag the item that you're interested in, get the brand, pull up like an e -commerce window, and be able to buy that thing right then. Social, on the short term, we're seeing things like Snapchat spectacles, which are, again, changing the point of view of video blogging from here on this device, to outward from your point of view, which is making things more personal, more interesting. One interesting application for AR social layer in the future is like a real -life status update. So, one application is like you go into a bar and maybe you take a book, because you're an introvert like me, and you actually want to read in a bar, and you don't want to talk to anybody, right? And so you could have a status update that says that. Or if you've had a couple drinks, you're feeling chatty, you could change your status so everybody would see that you're ready to mingle, right? I've got fitness and sports left, which are related but separate enough that I'm keeping them separate. Fitness, short term you could imagine custom workouts synced to things like your heart rate, your exertion level, your recovery, custom content delivered in things like smart mirrors, which I've seen, and other devices. And longer term, imagine having a holographic personal trainer who shows up right in the middle of your workout space, and you can have that person demo perfect squat form, or what is a burpee? And you can walk around and actually see that happen. So that's going to be great for your form. Or also things like, like you know how in Mario Kart you can race against your ghost of your past time trials? So imagine if you had like a workout ghost where you could see how hard you went in the past session and try to eclipse that. And then in sports, we hear a lot today in the AR realm around data, sort of like fantasy data, things that are like adding an additional information layer to the sports that we're already watching, like player stats and overlays. But to me, the more interesting application of AR is to the players themselves. So I think we hear about performance enhancing drugs today. We're going to hear more about performance enhancing tech in the future. Like if you're a baseball player and you're wearing an AR headset, can you identify a pitch and the type of pitch as it's coming to you? Do you know the velocity? And so we started to work on this device, which comes out of the prototyping and is a really nice little form factor. It's very inexpensive. They're coming in under $30. We just finished our Kickstarter. Today we finished our Kickstarter at AR4E and we successfully funded. It was really just to unlock scale so that we can start to send out to departments in computer science and people and coders who are experimenting, the guys at Unity at Mapbox, right, to see what bubbles up, right? Because there's an amazing amount of potential when you're limited by hardware and you're unable to access the expensive parts of the market that hinders growth. And what we would like to see, and here's a little infographic, this is just a little piece of art. This is the beam path. Very simple. You add the phone in, image bounces around, you get a field of view. We have a demo out on the floor, so come by and see it. It'll give you an idea of the screen size and the field of view size. Right now it's about 110 degrees. We really wanted to go after things like comfort, right? Being able to wear it for long durations, you know, really leverage the power of the phone, right? There's all this amazing computing going on on the phone and it's really everything from a productivity assistant to a visual tracker, a GPS navigator, all that stuff built in. And we wanted it accessible, right? So that way we can really start to realize this potential marketplace. The edges are where the cool stuff happens, right? It's not going to be top -down management that says, you know, make AR happen. And a lot of times people cannot afford, even in high -end innovation departments, to scale and deploy across a whole organization something that is a little bit more of a white glove experience. The, um, so we have two paths that we've embarked on. One is this hardware path where, um, we are developing not only this very simple form factor, but also moving into more sophisticated pieces of hardware and then also content, right? Because my training is in the arts and I am, consider myself a storyteller by nature, then the obvious, you know, sort of place in the market is to design experiences and to help people, uh, create a scale -like experience. That really does not, um, break their budget or, or create, uh, cost overruns. We have, um, oh, why thank you, Brenton. There's one of the headsets right there. Um, yeah, so we have, yeah, they're, they're really lightweight and easy. Um, so we have some hardware paths that we're embarking on. This is the first step, and it's a step back for us because of this curve in the market. There is this big, empty, unserved portion of the market where Kirk wants to train his firefighters in augmented reality right now. And again, the cost is prohibitive to do that on scale. How do you put everyone in the, in this room at a reasonable cost inside of a headset? Uh, but it does come out of experiments for much, um, more sophisticated glass -based, glasses -based technology. And our next moves will include a hard hat, a bike helmet, and a brimmed hat. So everything from the lowest end of the market to moving into kind of the Gear VR plastic daydream sort of world, right? Uh, again, because the phone is placed close to your head, it makes it easy to wear. It's light and comfortable. But then, that's only hardware and, you know, a platform for delivery. There's really this kind of unique sauce, which is the content creation. What do you do with it? Now, I think we've all seen amazing examples over the last few years of what you can do with it. And so, now is a chance, um, to really sort of break open the storytelling experiences. No longer will you need to hold your phone in your hand while you try and construct the Lego thing or try and do your unit of work. Now, with a headset and a mobile environment, you're able to exercise your productivity. And that becomes a little, I feel like that's a game changer, right? It starts to step into the market and say, you've been promised this augmented reality future, this glasses -based headset reality. Well, let's stimulate the very, um, beginnings of that with something that's accessible to everyone. Because I'm sure none of us really know what that killer app is going to be, right? We all had expected a killer app to break open VR. Now, VR is doing fine and it's growing, but it's not at the pace that we had expected. And I don't think that, I mean, there is a killer app. It's called Superhot. Thank you, Dotto, for introducing me to Superhot. If you haven't played Superhot, then please do. It's, it's, it's quite an experience. But then we also found that, you know, there were these amazing uses where we did mixed reality experiments, people holding a handrail while walking around a facility. That is so transformative. And now with the headset, you can see the world around you, right? So you're not just sort of locked in to this only single view, which removes eye strain. It's going to remove some of the spatial sickness that happens for a lot of people. Right? And it creates an easy way to continue to be in the world while having this other layer of information presented upon it. Right? So AR4E and my own company, ARX, we're kind of like joined forces in this content and hardware positioning. And we've been out shooting 360 video. We've been testing interfaces and lighting conditions to see what works and what doesn't and starting to learn best practices. Dennis and I, we joke a little bit about creating a content center of excellence. That there's really, but that's happening here at the media lab through guys like John, through events like this. We were kind of like right at the nexus of this tipping point in the marketplace where it's getting really interesting and very exciting. You know, building video games is not just the hat trick of augmented reality. That tool time training, the ability to have remote assistance, access to expertise or sensor fusion is really where it gets fun and exciting for day to day life. For really upgrading people's skills. I wanted to mention Seymour Papert and his constructionism kind of thinking, right? This idea that we're going to be able to unlock this power of learning because it no longer needs to be book bound linear type training, right? There's now the opportunity to go completely non -linear with your trainings, with your experiences. Video games have been accepted as a learning mode. There's no reason to hold back any longer, right? The thing that's been holding kind of the fat middle of this curve back has been access to hardware. The mobile phone is perfect for that. It's got a lot of power, right? It won't do all of the things that we want right out of the gate, but I think that's where the innovation will happen. And we know that this is kind of like, you know, the slogan, how do you eat an elephant one bite at a time? But this augmented reality, this market is an elephant and the projections are astronomical about its growth over the next just even five years, decade. So how do we attack this, right? Well, we're going to do it as a joint, as a group together. We will be able to dissect this thing and come up with solutions that serve the space. We've already begun to grab partnerships in medicine and defense, in industry and infrastructure. And one project I'd like to mention is my good friend, Aaron Riley, from the Annenberg School in New Media Literacy, is working to create these figital experiences, play -based experiences. And while I was with her in L.A. looking at the strategic scenarios of how this would work out,

[None]
it

[SPEAKER_00]
always broke when you had to hold up the phone. It limited the play, it limited the immersion in play. So what kind of came out of that was this real, and also conversations with guys like Kirk from last year, is there's this need to get something, an optic, that's accessible and easy to use, and pair that with some great content and pair that with best practices. How do you actually put a user interface in front of someone's face? What do you do when they are moving forward in space? How active or passive is the interface layer? What does it know about the user? We've talked broadly about use cases in entertainment, and this idea that the collective journey is starting to overtake this idea of the hero's journey. The hero's journey is still the individual's journey here on Earth. We now understand a broader market dynamic, and that is this collective journey. And if you watch movies critically, you'll see them playing to these broader group dynamics. The opportunity is now to play out the group dynamic as well as the individual one. The mobile phone, that mobile network, contains the information of you. So not only can you experience the catharsis of the group, but you can also experience your own individual piece of that with real resolution. That's pretty incredible. And we hope that you'll come and check out the demo. The headset's here. We'll throw a phone in it with one of the 360 videos, so you can get a sense of the optic. And please come and join us. Thank you. Thank you.
sources.title: “Just because you have a hammer…” AR use cases, and the mobile market | Steven Taylor | ARIA

I invest about 50 million dollars a year into 150 new startups every year. You said when an idea appears to be absolutely preposterous, that's when you like to get involved. I think that's an intriguing start for an investment. I actually love the expression, it's by Buckminster Fuller. If you really want to change something, don't fight the existing reality. Create a new model that makes the existing model obsolete. I was one of two people that came up with the term cloud computing. The idea was really to have software that was not running on your computer. The initial reaction was, why would I want to do that? I think that's the initial reaction for most people when they hear of a new technology. They actually just can't quite understand it yet. When they actually see it for the first time and it really works, it's basically magic. When you're looking at things that seem impossible, they actually have the possibility of becoming in fact inevitable. An area that I think is very important is in regenerative medicine. Printing tissues, printing organs, that can help restore life and eliminate disease. I have a son who's autistic. I would love to be involved in trying to create a way to have him be able to speak and to be able to interact and to live a full and meaningful life. I think it's miraculous what medicine has discovered so far about the human condition. We've seen so much of an advancement and a productivity rise for all of civilization in this in this last 30 -year period. What's now happening in the next 30 years is that same sort of Cambrian explosions through genetics, life sciences, connected hardware and hardware devices that are actually going to enable the human experience to be much more enriched in the coming years. I'm not scared of the advancement of science. Genetically modified organisms is sort of a throwback to like, oh wait, who originally created the genetics?
