[SPEAKER_01]
Welcome to Uncommons, a podcast focused on Canadian politics. I'm your host, Nathaniel Erskine -Smith. In this episode, we explore the health response to COVID -19. Do we have enough personal protective equipment? Are we mobilizing fast enough to scale up the testing and tracing required? I'm joined by Sarah Downey, the president and CEO of Michael Garron Hospital, our local hospital here in Beaches, East York. I'm later joined by Danielle Allen, professor and the director of the Ethics Center at Harvard University, leading a team of experts publishing white papers in response to the pandemic. First, here's my conversation with Sarah about the needs and experience of frontline healthcare workers and hospitals. Thanks, Sarah, for joining me. I really appreciate it in the context of everything you are doing. I appreciate you taking the time. And I also just at the outset just want to say how thankful I am and our community is for your work at Michael Garron Hospital and the work of all frontline healthcare workers who have, it's incredible what you are all doing on our behalf. So I just want to say thank you. And my first question, which is on, I think everyone's mind, is personal protective equipment. And do you at Michael Garron Hospital have the equipment that you need?

[SPEAKER_00]
So, Nate, there's a lot of elements to personal protective equipment. And as long as we continue to get the stock in every day and every week from our warehouses, then we have implemented a number of strategies to try to protect enough PPE. For today, we're fine. For this week, we're fine. But what worries us is really if we end up in a very large volume of COVID cases, will we have enough? So it's a multi -pronged question. And I would say today we're fine. Over the next week, I think we're fine. But we're trying to make sure we have the right stuff if we end up in a terrible place the way New York, for instance, has been.

[None]
But we've

[SPEAKER_01]
read about some Ontario hospitals that have said, we're going to see shortages. And obviously, we now see PPE thankfully coming into the country very quickly. And hopefully those shortages are not so dire. You at Michael Garron, though, have taken a number of steps to ensure that that kind of critical shortage doesn't happen quickly, among other steps I think that you've taken beyond PPE.

[SPEAKER_00]
Yeah. So, I mean, the one that people go to most is masks. So maybe I'll explain briefly our mask strategy. So as you know, we've done a community campaign to make masks, fabric masks. Here's one, for instance, beautiful masks. And we get regularly dropped off from across our neighborhoods, these fabulous masks, as done by the pattern that's on the Foundation's website. So our vision of these masks is that ultimately, every patient, every visitor that comes to Michael Garron for everything can wear these and be safe in our environment and protect our staff in case, for instance, they're asymptomatic for COVID and develop it later, they will have had a mask in our facility to protect people and they take them home if they wish or leave them and wash them. So for healthcare workers, we have for everybody, the surgical mask, which is this one, the ear loop mask. And this one, we get a little bit worried about, will there be enough surgical masks? And so we give every patient facing staff two of these a day.

[None]
We give every

[SPEAKER_00]
non patient facing staff one of these a day, people like me, and we use it. And if for instance, it got soiled or ripped or torn, we'd obviously replace it. But we've implemented, you know, guidelines to minimize the use. And then we have very specific guidelines in place for when you need the N95 mask. And therefore very specific procedures on patients who have COVID or suspected COVID, called aerosol generating medical procedures. And that's when you really need more protection than the surgical mask. so we have guidelines. In fact, the N95 masks we are collecting. After their use, we believe there will be approaches to sterilization and repurposing of them that we're looking for. And so between masking our community and our patients with these fabulous masks that our wonderful community members have done for us, rationing to some degree, but safely, the use of things like the surgical masks, and then the N95s are available when we really need them, has kind of been our approach. And if we can maintain this and our supplies continue in the way they have been every day and every week, then we think we'll be fine. The problem will be is if the warehouses are empty, and the N95s are stopped at the Canadian border. And so I think it's really important what our governments are doing is try to preserve the flow of stock to us so we can continue with these practices.

[None]
you

[SPEAKER_01]
are doing at the local level everything you can do to conserve PPE. then it fundamentally is up to us at the federal level and the provincial level working together to make sure you have the resources that you need on a going forward basis. But it's not just PPE that you have taken measures to protect at

[None]
Michael

[SPEAKER_01]
Garen.

[None]
You've

[SPEAKER_01]
also taken measures to make sure that COVID patients don't interact with other patients in your hospital.

[None]
Yeah,

[SPEAKER_00]
so we regularly see every day we diagnose people with COVID -19. Mercifully, fortunately, many are well and don't require admission. At the current moment, we have eight patients on our regular acute care units, and we put them together on a respiratory unit where we have specialized expertise. We have four in the intensive care unit. We actually have three going home today. So a lot of people are recovering from COVID. So currently, we haven't maxed out our capacity. We've canceled surgery to a large degree to create capacity for people who are very ill that need to come in, and we haven't had to enact all that yet. So we do. We have a respiratory unit. It gets very busy at times like the flu. They're experts in handling respiratory illnesses and contagious illnesses like COVID -19. And so that's where we cohort our patients currently. But we actually have a plan in our opening units that should we end up, you know, in a situation where we have a lot more COVID patients where we can create COVID units, non -COVID units. We require lots of testing to be able to, you know, separate those people because, of course, some people at the onset are asymptomatic. But really, we have a plan to convert our hospital to really a large acute care and ICU facility should we end up requiring it in the near future.

[SPEAKER_01]
And you mentioned the need for testing. And I just got to pause here a little bit because I was reading today's April 8th. And just yesterday, was reading Ontario on a per 100,000 residents is testing 563 people versus Alberta, almost three times that 1468, Quebec 1231. And we read that we are not even hitting the capacity that we have. Do you see testing the need for testing to scale up more quickly? And is it a matter of supplies? Is it a matter of human resources? What can be done to increase the scale of testing?

[SPEAKER_00]
Yeah, so we certainly need more testing, I would say that, mercifully, Michael Garan Hospital and a partnership we have in a lab with Sunnybrook North York and Scarborough Health Network created our own ability to do testing in our shared hospital lab, which is in North York. And so we have prioritized healthcare workers because we have to understand if they can get back to work. And we have screening at our doors for symptoms of COVID. So we do testing of healthcare workers and of inpatients to be able to properly protect our staff and provide the right care to COVID patients to keep it safe. We'd love to test every surgical patient. We'd love to test everybody in the emergency department. We'd love to test everybody who's shown up in our assessment center. We'd love to know that our communities are being tested. Does it exist in families? That has been the successful strategy of places like South Korea. That requires a public health intervention. But I know that we would love to test a lot more in the hospital. We've just have had limited capacity. And we need our test turnaround quickly. So we can't, you know, flood our limited capacity today.

[SPEAKER_01]
And what is the turnaround today? I read in South Korea about these drive -through testing centers that can turn the tests around in 10 minutes and you receive your results by text message. I don't know. We obviously are not there in Ontario.

[SPEAKER_00]
No, and that's not the testing we're doing in our lab. And I'm, you know, I'm not an expert in that test, but I'd love to have it here. When we send our tests to our shared hospital lab, we get the results in 24 to 48 hours, which we need to get healthcare workers back to work if they're COVID negative. And we need to understand the precautions required for inpatients that we are, that are suspect COVID patients to properly cohort and organize care for them differently.

[SPEAKER_01]
It seems testing is absolutely necessary, as you say, for healthcare professionals and, and to protect other patients in the hospital. But as we want to not only save lives in the course of this pandemic, but also return to some sense of normalcy in our society, testing becomes even more critical. And we ought to be looking at, you know, the numbers we're looking at today on testing are not going to get us to that sense of normalcy in any way whatsoever. So it seems that based on my own reading and consultations, I'm thinking PPE and testing ought to be the priorities. Is there anything else you would would say from a from a national level, I should be focused on my conversations with the health minister and others?

[SPEAKER_00]
Yeah, I mean, I think those are two really important topics. And to stabilize that would offer a lot of help and support. I think the public health measures and a continued focus on physical distancing, closure of non essential businesses, the school closures, all those things to try to flatten the curve, it remains incredibly important. We are not at the peak. You know, our estimates are it'll be weeks before a peak comes. And while we're not overwhelmed today, you know, you can have a bad day and you can be on a bad path. And that's what we're getting the hospital sector ready for, is should we, you know, diagnose more people with COVID than we have in the past. And we do watch, you know, we have we have modeling, we've looked at the provinces modeling that was released, just trying to be sure that we have a hospital capacity in place to deal with it, should our numbers increase dramatically. And so it's been important, you know, many organizations have, you know, given licenses to retired healthcare workers to be able to come back to work. They need to know that if they come back to work, they're safe with PPE, and responsible hospital practices. So I support that a number of things to try to get more workers, because that will be our rate limiting step, our workers. And then the other thing that would be good to have, which has been hard to procure has been ventilators. And again, these are global shortages, we see what happens in the world. And we certainly would love to have more ventilators to be able to increase our capacity in the ICUs. And we have a plan to go from our 17 bed ICU to 35 with existing equipment. But we'd love to be able to get to 50. And that would require actually having ventilators and the orders, even if we put them in today, the best guess is July or August for new ventilators to be able to come. So if we can source ventilator solutions locally, it'll give many of our people some reassurance that if it's needed, we can expand even more.

[SPEAKER_01]
And then the system won't be overwhelmed. I, in the east end here, we have seen some deaths we've seen. I mean, you mentioned your work expanding strategies at the hospital, but I know also you are, you and healthcare workers from MGH are in the community helping in long -term care facilities as well. And at St. Clair O 'Connor community, there have been four deaths from the most recent news that I've seen. And it's such a wonderful, such a wonderful home for so many and so tragically impacted. And the advice to people in the community, I mean, we, we, we have to physically distance, we have to stay home as much as reasonably possible so that people like you and our frontline healthcare workers are able to do the work safely. But are there other things we ought to be doing? I saw recently that Dr. Tam has suggested people should wear masks when out in public. Are there other things so that we don't see more deaths in our community and we keep our, our, our community safe?

[SPEAKER_00]
Right. So a few things. One is with this mask campaign, we hope that if we can stabilize our hospital supply, that we will put a mask on everybody in East Toronto. It our goal, and is to keep the army of sewers sewing so that everybody could get a mask. We really think that's vital. So when you go to the grocery store, when you're out for whatever reason, you can put it on and be safe. The long -term care home is, is perhaps the part that does worry us the most in the hospital sector. It's, it's really sad what's happened in homes like St. Clair O 'Connor. Of course, your seniors are the most vulnerable. They live in tight quarters. They have low staffing ratios anyway. They don't have the infection control standards and approaches that hospitals do. And so we've reached out to many of them in East Toronto to try it with our head of geriatrics, Dr. Jared Rosenberg, and our geriatric nurses and our long -term care outreach nurses to try to galvanize a response that better protects our seniors who live either in congregate living or in long -term care facilities. So we are working with a lot of local people to try to, to, to protect them. We are at St. Clair O 'Connor trying to keep people in place who have advanced directors and who wish to die in situ, not have to come to hospital, that kind of thing. But I would say that is the thing that worries me the most is the state of our seniors and the need to think both within the walls of Michael Garan that has, you know, a capacity and a skillset and wonderful people to deliver acute care, but also through partnership with others who also need to stand up a robust response. You know, they need access to PPE. They need access to cleaning products. They need access to our standards. They need access to our people many times. And so we're really working within our community to stretch the Michael Garan model outside the walls at 825 Coxwell into communities and neighborhoods when that is required, hoping it's never required, but in, in places like St. Clair O 'Connor, you know, we're there trying to help.

[None]
Well,

[SPEAKER_01]
I, when I see the work of Michael Garan to develop one of the first assessment centers in Ontario, when I see the work of Michael Garan to get out into the community to protect seniors, like at places like St. Clair O 'Connor community. And when I see that you're tripling assessment capacity, knowing that we, this is one of the critical areas of action. I just, I'm very thankful for everything you are doing. I encourage everyone to get out and, and contribute to the mask effort if they can. And do you have anything else you want to, you want to add? I mean, I'm just very thankful for everything you guys are doing.

[SPEAKER_00]
And, and we're thankful for this part of our community. You know, the PPE drive was amazing. And I know personal friends who dropped off supplies because they had them. And, uh, I can tell you the love of our community for Michael Garan Hospital has really been felt and it lifts our spirits to know that so many people out there are rooting for us and cheering for us and bang pots and pans for the healthcare workers. It does make us feel better. And to know that we're doing 100 % what we can to keep our community safe. And, uh, and so, um, thanks to everybody, uh, for all your moral support and we're happy to keep you posted on how we're doing inside.

[None]
And

[SPEAKER_01]
don't hesitate. I know so much of your work will ultimately depend upon the work of the federal government and the provincial government working in cooperation to make sure you have the resources, whether it's the testing capacity, the human resource capacity, or the PPE that you absolutely need. And so don't hesitate to be in touch with me and, and so that I can be a voice on your behalf as well.

[None]
And otherwise, thanks

[SPEAKER_01]
so much.

[SPEAKER_00]
Thank you, Nick. Take care.

[SPEAKER_01]
Next, here's my conversation with Professor Allen about the need to respond to this pandemic with a wartime effort. Danielle, thanks for joining me.

[SPEAKER_02]
Thank you so much for having me. glad to, glad to talk with you.

[SPEAKER_01]
And you, I was looking at your background. I first read your Washington Post op -ed from March 26th, calling for really strong mobilization action. But then when I went underneath that to the three white papers that your team has published, I then saw you have largely actually published in political theory, sociology, history, and how did you come to lead a team of experts in this health crisis?

[SPEAKER_02]
So thank you for that question. It gets to the heart of the matter. Um, so I direct, um, the Edmajay Staff Center for Ethics at Harvard, and we are a center that focuses broadly on ethics and public affairs. And what that means ultimately is that we try to support, if you don't mind my calling it this, sort of non -technocratic approaches to decision -making. What that means is we work really hard to build teams that bring multiple perspectives together, including technical expertise. But there's a real strong focus on making sure that we're putting together the people who are thinking about our overarching objectives, our core values, and so forth with the technical experts. So our method, our working method for years has been about coordinating different kinds of expertise. So when this problem, you know, emerged, there was a certain point where I reached out, um, to another colleague, Ezekiel Emanuel at Penn and said, how can we help? You know, we're an ethics center sitting here. This is what we need, know how to do. And he said, well, the hardest question right now is how to balance the sort of economic, um, costs and the public health, um, costs and so forth and how to have an integrated strategy. So we jumped in to trying to answer that specific question, but what that immediately made clear was that you had to answer a whole lot of other questions simultaneously. You really need an integrated policy framework. And so we started building out a network of people who could answer different parts of the puzzle.

[SPEAKER_01]
What a critical thing to do to build that team around you first. And so when it comes to public health experts, I was reading, I mean, obviously core competency as a matter of justice and morals and an ethicist, but

[None]
you're surrounded

[SPEAKER_01]
by a team of public health experts to lean on to ensure you've got the best evidence at your disposal.

[SPEAKER_02]
Absolutely. We wouldn't say anything, make any arguments without being sure that we absolutely were up to speed with the state of art scientific understanding. So we're really lucky at Harvard to have access to leading researchers at the Chan School of Public Health. So for example, Mark Lipsitch and Rebecca Kahn, we've been checking in with them repeatedly and we make one of our basic practices as a sort of weekly matter to get a briefing about, well, what are the most recent scientific papers? How should we think about asymptomatic cases and case presentation? How should we think about immunity? When will, what's the timetable for really understanding immunity, et cetera, the whole range of it. So, I mean, that is really, it's sort of like, I think of it a bit as being about a sort of symphony conductor. You really, you absolutely need that state of the art scientific expertise. But at the same time, I think one of the things I've learned that's been most powerful is that public health modelers, as they got into modeling responses to this, very often in their models, sort of built in a status quo picture of socioeconomic realities. So, in some sense, they modeled around the current level of capacity for testing that, say, Canada or the US happens to have.

[None]
And so it

[SPEAKER_02]
became clear that what we needed was, well, if you could completely transform the infrastructure for delivering testing, well, how then do we model the public health strategies? And you have to sort of be able to integrate that sort of socioeconomic transformation piece, infrastructure investment piece with the public health strategies. And so that's what we're trying to do.

[SPEAKER_01]
And it's a or an interesting point about testing and taking a step back and saying it's not about existing capacity, it's about reshaping and mobilizing to blow the current capacity out of the water and expand it to such a large degree, given the scale of the pandemic that we have. And when I look at South Korea as an example that I read about quite a lot, but even I see what's happening in Germany right now.

[None]
You

[SPEAKER_01]
wrote about mobilize and transition in your piece, and we see countries doing that, I think, to some extent.

[SPEAKER_02]
Absolutely. I mean, I think across Europe, we're seeing countries have transitioned to embrace of a mobilizing transition paradigm, where the goal is to transition to pandemic resilience. And what that really means is that you have the capacity to see the disease through massive testing, and to treat it and to quarantine people who have the disease and so forth. that currently, we use a combination of social distancing, stay at home orders and so forth, things like testing to try to decelerate the rate of transmission and bring ourselves back to a place where the transmission rate is below one, and back to a place where our hospitals can handle treatment of severe cases. And then ideally, once we're back at that place, we can, we will have built up, we will have mobilized and invested in a sort of testing infrastructure that permits us to control the disease over time. And that's what pandemic resilience is about, really. So we're not talking about eliminating the disease. I think that's been one of the hard things in this conversation. Lots of public health strategies are focused on containment, which has the goal really of elimination. At this point, we have such prevalence that elimination is not a real possibility.

[None]
So we have

[SPEAKER_02]
to understand the kind of control that nonetheless permits us to keep our economy working. And the key to that is really the testing and contact tracing regime.

[SPEAKER_01]
After reading your work, I then saw information coming out of Germany that they're testing not only people who have symptoms, but they're testing more randomly within the population at large, both to get a sense of where they're at, but also to ensure that they identify people who have had the disease, who can then come back and proactively support the economy.

[SPEAKER_02]
Exactly, that's exactly what we should be doing. while we're in this phase of collective social distancing, which we absolutely need right now, we should also be testing broadly in order to exempt some people from those stay -at -home orders. So anybody who's already immune should be exempted. So the tricky thing is we don't actually have a full picture of immunity yet. It's not clear how long immunity lasts, for example, so we're still learning about that. So the tests for a negative sort of presence of the virus are equally important. And so what you really need is a regime that can test critical workers who are exempt from stay -at -home orders on a sort of every two or three day basis to make sure that they stay free from the virus. But that is a hugely important thing to getting the economy going again. Because if you think about it, what we've got, you know, at the moment is sort of 90 % of the population staying at home, but that 90 % of the population, only one to 2 % is actually carrying the virus. So

[None]
the question

[SPEAKER_02]
is, how can we get as many people out as possible?

[None]
It's

[SPEAKER_01]
clear that ramping up testing and ensuring that for elderly care, for child care, and for various critical services for vulnerable populations, that we are able to test people quickly. Healthcare frontline workers, the most obvious one, but we're able to test people quickly and regularly and have the capacity, not just capacity for testing kids, which is, which, but the big takeaway from your work was the supply chain and human resources to make that happen at the same time.

[SPEAKER_02]
Exactly. It is a big logistical piece of work, no question about it. That's the sense in which the right metaphor is putting a country on a war footing. It is immobilizing parts of the economy, redeploying labor. It is about achieving enough coordination sort of at a national level to ensure that supply chain, all the way from the test production to distribution and last mile test administration. I think there's lots of room for jurisdictional authority at all the levels of a federal structure. And I think that's a good thing. I think our federal structures are flexible and adaptable that are an asset to us. We have to figure out how to activate them as an asset, even in that context. So I think the important thing to say is that we need all parts of our federal structures working together, including the national part. So federalism is great. It gives us that flexibility and adaptability. It works best when all of its layers, federal, state, municipal, and so forth, are working in coordination with each other.

[None]
Yeah.

[SPEAKER_01]
without too great of a comment, I do feel lucky to live in Canada for that reason alone. No

[None]
comment on

[SPEAKER_01]
your part. That's okay.

[None]
No comment on my part. We're working on

[SPEAKER_02]
it. I have confidence in us. We're going to get there.

[SPEAKER_01]
When it comes to, I mean, I could ask you about just the notion of Medicare for all too. As a Canadian, I can't think of a better example for Medicare for all than something like this. But I want to get to this. One last question on this notion of mobilizing in a wartime footing. And you make note, permits maximum mobility for as large a portion of the population as possible. That has to be the right answer. And when it comes to a wartime footing, are we at the point of working collaboratively with companies? Or are we at the point of really centralizing decision making to make things happen in a fast way given the scope of the efforts that need to happen?

[SPEAKER_02]
So we've been digging into the history of World War II a little bit to try to understand that, to try to understand what the best structures are. And I think where we're landing at the moment, I mean, the work is still ongoing, is the notion that something like the War Production Board, which was a private partner collaboration, would be the right structure. So we do need leading firms to come together into a coordinated entity, but they really need to do that working under the direction of senior elected leadership and policymakers. So in that regard, I think it's not a sort of de -registre -model. It's not a sort of that's nationalized supply chains and so forth. It really is about the elected officials working to pull together that what we call testing supply board to get that production, that supply line organized and make sure all the parts of it get the support they need and get the public investment they need. So that's the other really important role on the part of the national government is to funnel public investment into that supply chain so that it's functional and all the pieces have confidence and can coordinate in relationship to each other, knowing that the whole structure will get that funding injection.

[SPEAKER_01]
Thanks to Professor Allen for joining us. You can find the white papers from her team on the website for Harvard Center for Ethics. And a big thank you, of course, to Sarah Downey and her team of frontline health professionals for everything that they're doing in our community out of Michael Garan. You can find out more information about their efforts and how to help their efforts at both the foundation's website and the hospital's website. And lastly, remember to subscribe at uncommons.ca for future episodes, including episodes with Elizabeth May and Hedy Frye. learning

Hello and good morning. I got a couple of props here I'm going to use in the course of my talk this morning. But real quick, I'm the CEO of PTC. PTC is a fairly large software company based in the Boston area here out in Needham to be precise. And we've been doing a lot in IoT and AR and I wanted to share some of that with you because I think it's pretty exciting and a lot of it's real. You know we're engaged with about a thousand companies right now on the intersection industrial you know B2B customers at the intersection of IoT and AR. And really my thesis here is that the more you talk about IoT the more you're kind of magnetically drawn towards AR. And I'll try to explain why I think that happens. But I think that AR is going to be a critical enabler for us to get the full value out of IoT. So you might be thinking PTC isn't that an old CAD company? And I'd say yeah you know in the same way that MIT is an old university. But even old universities work on new ideas and at PTC an important event happened about seven years ago which is the board of directors decided that the new CEO should be a technologist and they selected me the CTO to become the new CEO of PTC. And sort of with that mandate to you know let's say speed it up a little bit or add some more action to the company we went out and did a lot of crazy things and I just want to explain them. A big milestone happened last summer when we adopted this new logo to describe our company what we're trying to do. And it's a P for physical on top of a D for digital. And it's really built on this yin yang concept. So yin yang if you know it is is an Asian concept of two opposing forces that actually add quite a bit of value to each other and create some greater whole. know night and day, hot and cold, male and female, that kind of thing. So if you look at PTC we started as a CAD and PLM and ALM company helping customers to design products in the digital world to create high fidelity digital prototypes because it's too darn hard to iterate in the physical world. If you build a physical prototype and change your mind, that's a problem. Big expensive long process to change that physical prototype and so forth. So we can iterate for a long time, get it just perfect and then when we're ready we're going to cross the boundary. We could do that with 3D printing. Of course, that's a technology that's getting a second wave of interest right now as people go from printing throwaway prototypes to printing production parts that go right, you know, onto the manufactured product. But more typically you'd be doing this in a factory, a subtractive type of process where you're machining things down or injecting plastic into molds or what have you. And more and more IOT and AR are playing a role in what factories do and I'll probably touch on that a little bit later in the talk. But that's the second way to get from a digital idea to a physical product. Now at PTC, we always wished that we knew what was going on with the product after it left the factory because then we could more properly do product lifecycle management. It's a little hard to do lifecycle management for something you haven't seen in years or possibly even in decades. And that's ultimately what led us to make a series of acquisitions and investments around a brand we call ThingWorx so that we could get data back from the physical world and integrate it with our understanding of those same things from the digital world to create this concept we call a digital twin. So a digital twin would be like the avatar for something physical or the proxy. So by consulting this digital twin, you can see how the product is used and problem it's having and so forth and ultimately use that to improve the design. We also got into service software some years ago thinking that all this engineering data was important for service. Well, turns out nothing's more important for service than an understanding of the condition and the status and the use of some asset out in the field. So of course, IoT and analytics and the digital twin helps us think about how to optimize the service process to make it proactive, preventative, efficient, what have you. Now, what led us into AR was an understanding that many times you do have to go into the field and you have this rich information in your digital twin. Sure would be great if there were a way to bring that into the field and put it in the context of the physical product that you're trying to repair or optimize or what have you. And we also saw that virtual reality gives you a way to do that too, but with a virtualized replacement of the physical product, but still get the benefit of all the in context processing of this information. So this is sort of what PTC is doing right now. You can see we've come a long way from CAD, but everything we're doing still kind of seems to make sense together. And just for fun, I wanted to show you my first little demo here to try to prove out that concept I just showed you. And I'm going to run a piece of software that we call a Thing Browser. This is our Thing Works Thing Browser. And before I go any farther, let me say that this thing I have in my hand is actually a hydraulic pump from a Bobcat skid steer. It turns engine power into hydraulic pressure so that you can operate the bucket and so forth on a skid steer. Because what you see if you compare that screenshot to the pump I have in my hand is that it's a mixed mode assembly. It's part physical, it's part digital. And then what I can't show you is that the buttons along the bottom, which would be voice commands on the HoloLens, allow you to do things like say disassemble it and it comes apart. Show me the sensors, and there's a series of sensor readings on there. Show me the internals. And it turns out that because this pump, because it's 3D printed, it wouldn't be this way in the real world. But because it's 3D printed, it has a lattice structure inside. It's not solid. So we'd be able to see the x -ray vision of the lattice structure and so forth. So I'll save that because it's not that interesting without the demo. All right. So what's happened over the last couple of years with me personally, in addition to working on all that stuff at PTC, I've engaged in a couple of research projects with Professor Porter from Harvard around IoT. And that's led to two papers which we've published in the last couple of years. And another one that's underway, and this third one really is about AR and its influence on IoT in business. And I think you'll enjoy it when it's done. It's kind of in the final editing mode right now. But basically, the story starts out with the idea that more and more things in the world, even this tennis racket, are becoming smart and connected. And so this tennis racket has sensors in the handle, an accelerometer and an electronic gyroscope. It gathers data from those sensors, uses Bluetooth over to your phone, your phone up to the cloud. In the cloud, there's a database of sorts gathering together all the tennis rackets around the world. We're running analytics on them to figure out how your game is evolving, but also how your game compares to everybody else's game. And then we're delivering that back to the end user in traditional mobile applications. So this is a big idea. It's being applied even to tennis rackets. It creates tremendous amount of value because now we can monitor what's going on, even remotely, for things that we used to have no idea. We can, in some cases, have a control loop and be able to change or give feedback to that thing. You could imagine that tennis racket at a minimum buzzing. It's a little hard to control the tennis racket. But same way your phone has a buzz for an incoming call and a different buzz for an incoming text, we could remind you of certain things in your game even while you're playing. But with assets in general, let's say industrial assets, we can do dramatic things to optimize their use and their availability. And then we might even think about giving them the ability to make their own decisions and become autonomous and start optimizing themselves. So when products go from being not connected to being connected, you know, amazing things happen. But one of the things I've observed is that there's something missing. And that is while the tennis racket is part physical and part digital, I don't actually see it that way. Because when I look at it here, I see only the physical tennis racket. And when I look at it here, I see digital information about the tennis racket, but not in the context of the tennis racket. And it seems sensible that I would want to do this and see the two together. And to say, why can't you show me what's happening with that object in the context of that object by taking all the data you got from the sensors and putting it back in the context of the actual object? So in order to do that, we would just park a second stack of technology alongside that first stack. And that's really why I showed you the first stack, was to point out that we humans like to communicate with two channels, sound and vision. And it's actually very important. You know, that's why it's not that interesting to listen to somebody you can't see. And it's not that interesting to see somebody you can't hear. It's very interesting to get both of these channels because they bring in something separate. They have different capabilities, but they're also used to quality check each other. You know, if I say, you're my best friend, you're thinking, I don't think so. There's something about what I see that doesn't match, you know, what you say. So it's a powerful idea, but now we can put that idea on the physical world. We can gather data through IoT and sensors and analytics and using computer vision, see that object, recognize it, map all the data we gathered through IoT and analytics onto it, and then show it back to you in the context of the object. So I think it's a big, powerful idea to put those two together and to allow humans to have the data and visual link with the physical world that we love to have with each other to sort of optimize the full communication back and forth. Now, to be clear, I'm not really talking about tennis rackets here. I'm talking about everything in the physical world. It's worth noting that you have the same problem in your car. You know, when you're looking through the windscreen, you don't benefit from the digital information. And when you look down at the dashboard at your navigation system, you now have a set of information that's very important to you. But number one, you first have to understand it, because it's not in context. Is that green road? Is that I -90? Or is that Memorial Drive? Which one is it? You have to understand the scale. Then you have to remember it and then turn around and map it onto the physical world ahead of you so you know which road to turn on in order to get here this morning. And I was just going through this process as I drove in from the suburbs this morning. It's a difficult process in traffic and so forth. And wouldn't it be great if we could merge these ideas together and produce what you'd call a heads -up display? And of course, we can. We all know what heads -up displays are. It's just today, it's very costly and specialized to have something with a heads -up display. But to the extent that glasses or eyewear or maybe in a lot of cases mobile devices can integrate what I see with the data I need to know and act on, I suddenly have a heads -up display on everything. And that's a big powerful idea. It also solves another problem, which is the way we're headed today. Every thing thinks it's going to get to have its own apps. And I don't think that's really practical. I mean, I don't know about you, but if everything I interact with follows the lead of my swimming pool and my solar system and my smart home, I'm going to be swimming in apps. And when I want to interact with something, the first thing I'm to have to do is flip through 100 pages of apps to find which app is it that interacts with this thing. And I think this idea of augmented reality gives us a different approach, which is the ability to just figure out what you need to know and deliver it to you. So that's kind of the big idea that we're working on, which is if you start at the one o 'clock position here, we want to connect to the physical world, both to sensors, but also to automation and control systems. Because there's a lot of systems out there that already know things at the edge. We want to draw this data in from the edge and apply analytics to it. Analytics could be big data analytics, could be engineering simulation codes, could be business rules, what have you. But we want to say, what is that data telling us that we need to know in this context? And the context is, who am I? What role am I performing right now as it relates to this physical world in front of me? What do I need as this person performing this role to know and in what order of priority? And then what I want to do is decorate the physical world with what you need to know, maybe giving some level of priority indication. Throw everything else away because you don't need to know it and allow you to just simply engage that world with these two channels and see that decorated world that, you know, is the physical world with the heads up display kind of worn on my head. So I think this is a big idea, how IoT and AR work together. Like I said, we have about a thousand B2B customers just in the last two, two and a half quarters who have used our software to go prototype this kind of concept. There's a huge amount of interest out there. Again, our role at PDC is software. We're trying to provide the software infrastructure and plumbing to make all this happen and, of course, work with phones, tablets, eyewear from whomever, you know, makes the best. I want to show you a couple of ideas how this works, actual real customer examples. This service scenario is from a customer of ours called Sysmex. Sysmex makes blood and urine analyzers that you see in a hospital. So what's trying to happen here is that the blood technician, not the service technician, the blood technician, gets an alert from the machine that says, I have a clog, what's called an RBC clog. I don't know, that's probably a consumable flow is being clogged. And he gets that on his industrialized iPad, actually. And so through IoT, he's getting feedback from the machine and he presses a button that says, run the cleaning cycle. And so the self -cleaning cycle runs and it completes and says, sorry, I was unable to clear the clog. We're going to have to revert to a manual procedure. Now, at this point, I need to call a service technician or I need to be coached through the process. So what we would show you here is how AR and hopefully some of my other colleagues throughout the day here, we'll be able to show you how AR would coach this blood technician through a modest disassembly pipe cleaner type cleaning process of an orifice, reassemble the thing, run the self -check, and there you are back online again. With the idea that if this machine can't be fixed right now, you know, first of all, it's going to cost a lot of money to have a service technician come. Secondarily, it may be down for a day or two or three. And at the clinic, we've got a whole list of appointments that are kind of expecting this machine to run. So it's very expensive and inconvenient and even brand damaging to have this machine out of commission. But AR coupled with IoT can get to the basis of what is the problem, what would you need to do to fix the problem, and then let me actually visually coach you through the sequence of doing the things you need to do. Okay, let's try a manufacturing scenario. And this is a manufacturing training scenario. So you see there's a cylinder sitting on a plate, and there's some markers on there to help the camera know exactly where it is. And what you can't quite see or you can barely see a red tip device, which is the welding rod holder. I don't know what you call that thing. So this red handled device would be the welding rod. And we're using sensors to detect where is it, how much pressure is being applied, and at what speed and in what direction is it being moved. And then simulating what sort of weld that would generate, and then augmenting that weld onto the work material. And the idea here is it's very safe welding. It doesn't burn through consumable rods. It doesn't burn through consumable fixtures and parts. It's just a great way to sort of visually understand what you would see if you were actually doing that. Welding. And then a third example, which has less IoT in it, if we can flip to it, is sort of in the engineering world. So here's a case where we've taken a steel chassis, and we're going to grab CAD data off the screen and augment it into the right place on the steel chassis. And then again, this one was done probably on a tablet. We're walking around the chassis. We might even say, give me a different design, different design variant. There we go. That's a different design. So we're taking CAD data and augmenting it onto a physical assembly to produce a new assembly that's part physical, part digital, to allow us to iterate and say, you know, do we like that? Is that the one you want before I commit the factory to building it? Okay. So what I tried to show you there, if we jump ahead, was some examples in service, in factory, in engineering that use these ideas together. I want to talk a little bit about my theory of why it's important. Data, for example, from IDC says that the amount of data available to mankind is growing, as you know, at an enormous rate. And of course, IoT is a massive new source of data. So we have more data than ever that we want to be able to share, you know, with humanity. But we have a bit of a problem, which is the pipe into humanity is very small. And in fact, if you were to look at this phone there, that's the user interface for my swimming pool. And it's just text, you know, that you have to look at, read, and really all you get is the green indicator of the buttons on or off. But I would argue, I do argue, that we can only consume that type of user interface at three words per second. And I say that by saying we measure time, actually, by saying 1001. That's one second, three words. And very few people can speak faster than that, not much faster. And very few people can read dramatically faster than they can speak. And, you you can kind of prove that by handing somebody a paragraph and say, read it out loud. So I think your ability to read and visually process the symbology of text is somewhere around three words per minute. Okay, now this is the first part of Heppelman's Theorem. The second part is I remember being taught a long time ago that a picture is worth a thousand words. And, you we can study that. I don't know if it's worth a thousand or 900 or 1100. But there is a huge amount of rich information you can get in one second graphically. For example, if you closed your eyes, opened them for one second, looked around and closed them again, if you could remember everything you saw, it would take far more than a thousand words to describe it in text or to say it verbally. So I'm going to just take for granted that a picture is worth a thousand words. And then I'm going to take for granted that I can throw 60 pictures a second at you, and you pretty much process all of them. Notice all the little subtle differences and so forth. And you do that every time you're watching TV or sitting in front of your computer or anything else that runs at 60 hertz. So 60 hertz is, as you know, 60 pictures per second. So now I'm saying I actually could do a thousand words times 60. Now, not completely because if everything changed in those pictures, you'd have a harder time processing them. But if I could now not try to funnel it through a tiny little window in front of you, but actually make it part of your peripheral vision, because we see so much more than we have immediately in front of us, and we process it so fast using peripheral, you know, system one type of processing. I think that would gross it up by a hundred. And I say that only because I could imagine five more of them this way, five more of them that way, you know, five more that way, five more that way. Okay, I should make it a circle rather than a square. But anyway, that would give you a hundred times more ability to input if you were processing graphics through a, you know, smart glasses type of experience that allowed you through your peripheral vision. A lot of them today don't quite get out to your peripheral vision because of this narrow field of view problem, but, you know, I think that's where we're headed. So if you just do the math on that, you know, we could give you information two million times faster by feeding you graphical in -context information through your peripheral and focused vision than we can by putting text in an app on an iPhone. And that's a big, big idea if we really want to figure out how to make all the information available to us from the IoT more consumable and valuable. So that's the end of my talk. I wanted to close just with one last thing. Which is, we, PTC, are hosting a very big event here in Boston in, I think it's in May this year. Yeah, May 22nd, called Liveworks. It's really about that yin -yang, all that stuff I talked about, heavy dose on IoT, analytics, AR, VR, lots of partners. I expect we'll have about 10,000 people. And I hope to see, you know, many of you there as partners exhibiting your own ideas, attending, learning what's going on, and so forth. It'll be at the Boston Convention Center. And I invite you all to come. So thank you very much. Thank you. Thank you.

Racism in my experience is not just an American problem it's a human disease. I've lived in three US states and I've seen racism in each of these places against people of color, Latinx and other minority groups. I have spent six years living in Europe. As a child in France I saw firsthand racism against North Africans I went to school with who migrated to Europe. As a teenager in Germany I saw racism of the past visiting the Dachau concentration camp and I saw racism in the current day against Turkish immigrants who lived in our small town. While living in New Zealand in my early 20s I saw many instances of racism and bias against indigenous Maori and Polynesian populations. It's on each of us to stomp out racism inside and around us. I didn't know what to do so I switched to psychology as a major and I would just tell people psychology was so broad it would apply to anything I decided to do in my future. So come junior year my parents sat me down and had the inevitable discussion about how I really needed some direction in my life because I wasn't going to be on their payroll forever. Unfortunately for me that conversation coincided with my first constitutional law class and I had the best teacher Lee Epstein in college. So in my com law class we would have to read a new case or two before every class and we would have to be prepared to argue both sides of the case. We wouldn't know what side we would be on until we showed up for class the next day. So sometimes plaintiffs would be in the front, sometimes they'd be in the back, sometimes on the left or sometimes on the right. And what I learned through the whole constitutional law class that semester was that instead of liking things being black and white and always having an answer, I liked being able to figure out how to argue both sides. And also what I learned was that if you are prepared to argue both sides to something when you actually do have to pick one side to advocate for, your argument is that much stronger because you could predict what the other person on the other side is going to say. So I ended up going to law school and after law school I totally randomly fell into an insurance and to insurance and I was in private law practice representing insurance carriers. They were all financial lines insurance carriers which is exactly what I'm here to talk about. So we're not talking about health insurance, there's very little emotion involved, we're not talking about hurting a person because we're not providing coverage. But I fell into this and we would represent insurance companies and they wouldn't hire us to help them figure out how to deny coverage for a claim. But they would help us to try to figure out exactly what their contractual obligations were. So the way I look at it, an insurance policy is a contract and sometimes insurance carriers pay claims because it's black and white, sometimes they don't if it's black and white and there's then there's this huge gray area. And being able to argue whether you represent an insurance carrier or not, being able to argue why your argument should win is always really a great thing to have to do. So five years ago I left private practice and I joined Marsh which is an insurance broker and I now get to advocate for companies like you. So I'm on the opposite side from insurance carriers and I have seen nothing different than what I expected. The carriers aren't out to deny coverage every time, they're really trying to figure out how to apply the terms of their contract. So I tried to figure out how to make this seem more personal to all of you. So let's say you're a custodian and we have some type of contract agreement, something in place, I give you my digital assets. A year later the value goes down, that's fine, I can blame it on the market, that's not your fault. But when I go to withdraw my money, I'm really angry because there's no interest involved. I just get back the value of my coins or currency at the moment and I ask you for interest and you show me the terms of our agreement that say I paid only for you to hold my assets, not for you to put it in some type of interest bearing account. So just like your business, you don't want to pay for more than you have to pay. Insurers don't want to pay for more than that what they have to pay for. So it's kind of the same thing. So that's a long way of saying insurers do pay claims. And in fact over the last five years since I've been at Marsh, I tried to figure out how much I knew that insurance carriers had actually paid for clients that I work closely with. And I tried to figure it out quickly and my numbers are very, very rough. The number is definitely higher because I really only added in like the bigger payments and things like that. But I calculated that for the clients that I've worked with for the last five years, we've collected over $700 million in insurance proceeds for those clients. And I'm pretty sure if I counted all the small payments, the clients that I've forgotten about, I am pretty sure that number will be way closer to a billion dollars. And I'm one person out of about 300 people in my division. And so think about the, you know, the 700, 750 million dollar payment times 300. So the reason I wanted to share those stories with you is because if I can't convince you that insurance pays or to at least keep an open mind, then the rest of this discussion is going to be meaningless. And I didn't want that to happen. So hopefully at least you can keep an open mind about insurance. So who we are, we're a leading insurance broker. We don't provide insurance coverage. We help clients find the right insurance partners to work with. The insurance carriers then provide coverage to our clients. Insurance is a form of risk transfer. Companies in all spaces are exposed to various forms of liability based on the services they provide. Insurance helps transfer that risk away from the company's balance sheets onto the insurance carrier's balance sheets. Financial and professional lines insurance pays things like defense costs, settlements, judgments, various forms of liability exposure. Marsh as a broker helps clients obtain the necessary coverage. Based on your business model, we help you evaluate what coverages you need, how much coverage you need. We talk about policy wording and we make sure you have what you need to protect your business. We work with public companies, private companies, nonprofits, companies of all different sizes. We've seen it all. But what I am so fortunate to have the opportunity to do and the reason that I'm actually up here today is I have learned that when you have a new asset class or a new type of technology, new exposures, you actually have to create an insurance market. So I'm not talking about new insurance carriers because we have a whole bunch of traditional old school insurance carriers that we know pay claims and are very financially solvent. But we have to explain to those carriers and educate those carriers about blockchain technology and digital assets, what the real risk exposures are and if there are any different risk exposures than from a more normal, more traditional company or form of currency or assets. So at Marsh, we formed our DART team. We love our acronyms. It stands for Digital Asset Risk Transfer Team. And those of us in this space, there's a team of about 15 of us in the U.S. We're focused on working with top clients in the digital asset space to help them obtain the coverage they need, but also to educate the insurance market so that we can create capacity for others in the space who will need it eventually. So now moving on to the fun stuff, blockchain technology and digital assets, the top 10 reasons why insurance matters and why you need insurance. So reason number 10, to manage your employee exposure. So unfortunately, with all of blockchain's innovations and benefits, the technology has not solved the employment -related issues that are out there. So think sexual harassment, discrimination, retaliation. And this, of course, is relevant across all types of businesses, but for companies who are new and who are focusing on blockchain and digital assets, they likely have little investment made into their employment -related policies. They probably don't have a human resources department. They also probably have smaller balance sheets. Employment claims in general are really easy to file and to bring, even though the costs of those suits are generally relatively small, they're so high in volume that the numbers add up very quickly. So for a new company, instead of carrying that risk on their balance sheet, why not transfer it to an insurance company's balance sheet? Reason number nine, key individuals need protection too. So here I'm thinking about kidnap and ransom insurance. So this is the most fun type of insurance to talk about, definitely the least fun type of insurance to rely on, because you never hope you're in this situation. But there is actually insurance for kidnap and ransom. So in this space, think about the fact that there's a select group of individuals who hold the private keys or who hold information that control access to digital assets. Plus, think about all the wealth that all these individuals have in the space right now. There is a very high probability that K &R coverage or kidnap and ransom coverage could come in handy one day. It's very affordable coverage. All of the coverages that I'm going to talk about are basically a year. K &R coverage you can actually buy for three years. And it provides exactly what it says, coverage for kidnap and ransom situations, but a ton of other things like threat response and corporate and personal security experts, things that smaller, newer companies may not already have access to. Reason number eight, it could be required by contract. So here I'm talking about what we refer to as miscellaneous professional liability coverage, or Arizona admissions coverage, E &O coverage. So professional liability or E &O coverage basically provides coverage for claims arising out of the professional services you provide to your clients for a fee. So there are many contracts that you might have with outside vendors or partners probably require that you purchase E &O coverage. So think about this. If you provide advisory services to startups in this space, if the company you advise were to sue you because your advice was somehow deficient, you would want your own protection. You would want insurance to pay for that claim. You wouldn't want to have to carry that cost by yourself. Similarly, the startup may require that you have your own E &O coverage because if for whatever reason you refuse to pay the claim or you become insolvent, they want to know that there's insurance there as a backstop. Number seven, tech errors happen. Should a digital currency or smart contract not behave as promised, the technology or software developer could face significant liability. The number of these claims has increased in recent years as technology investments have accelerated. And tech E &O helps transfer the exposure for these type of tech issues from your company's balance sheet to that of the insurance carriers. Number six, could be required by law or regulation. So depending on the structure of your company, whether you're a trust company, a 40 act fund or a broker dealer, there could be requirements that you obtain certain kinds of insurance. And here we're thinking about types of bonds, whether it's FI bonds or financial institution bonds, or risk bonds or surety bonds. Sometimes certain types of insurance may actually be required for your business. Reason number five, ensure against business interruption and other breach issues. Cyber insurance does a number of things, including covering first party breach, business interruption costs and breach notification costs. So if you hold PII or personally identifiable information for your customers and there's a breach, cyber insurance could help you. Number four, protect your customers' assets and it could also be a great marketing tool. Here we're talking about crime or fidelity coverage. So think theft of assets or hacks. Crime coverage can protect assets in cold, warm or hot storage, assuming the insurance policy is structured correctly. There's a ton of press about certain companies working with digital assets that use the fact that they have crime coverage as a marketing tool. Please read the policies at issue very, very carefully. They really can protect a customer's assets, but the typical crime policy is actually structured to protect the company who buys the policy's own assets that they're holding. And so the customers tend not to be the lost beneficiaries or payees. So when you see those articles, please do your homework. Protect your personal assets and attract top talent along the way. DNO insurance protects the directors and officers of companies sued if they're sued or involved in some type of regulatory action. It's often referred to as the last line of defense and best form of personal asset protection. So if the company you work for is unable or refuses to indemnify you and you happen to be sued or involved in some type of regulatory investigation, you don't want to have to start paying your own defense costs. So DNO insurance is there to protect yourself. Plus, it's a great way to attract talent along the way. With newer companies, many of you are focused more on the tech side, so you bring in outside support advisors who have more business experience. Experienced directors oftentimes require DNO insurance. So why not show them that you already have this in place? Protect your balance sheet. DNO insurance can also protect the company itself if the company does something wrong, if they're sued, if the company is involved in a regulatory investigation. So DNO insurance really protects the individuals and the companies. And finally, the number one reason why insurance matters to the advancement of blockchain technology and digital assets is insurance because it supports growth and innovation. It's involved in every industry out there. Amongst other things, it helps increase the brand behind an industry. There's a stringent underwriting process which makes regulators, banks, and investors comfortable knowing that if they're looking at a company that has insurance, someone else tested their procedures and they're comfortable with this company. Banks and outside investors will see you as a better investment if you have insurance, so you can get the capital to do the things you need to innovate and grow. And if there is a loss, you have the safety net to stay afloat and continue to grow where others lag behind. And I've actually seen many companies thrive because they have the support of insurance and I've seen smaller companies fail because they don't have insurance in place. I'll just quickly touch on why insurance needs you. Insurance underwriters like data. Because this is a new space, new technology, and new assets, there's very little lost data out there. Newer companies have very little financial history, so the underwriters are uncomfortable in the space. And when uncomfortable, insurers act very conservatively. Either they don't provide coverage, they price it really high, or they limit the coverage. And this is where great partnerships come in handy. So we've worked very hard to educate the insurance markets. We've brought in outside law firms to help us through educational events with some of the top US markets and London markets. We've also been fortunate enough to have some amazing clients in this space, some of you are in this audience, who have either helped with our events or through their own underwriting meetings, their own attempt to obtain coverage for themselves. They've really devoted the time to teaching the insurers about their technology and the exposures that are associated with what they're doing. And also with some in the audience too, we've already formed strategic partnerships and we're in the process of forming a few more. We've with companies who can help bring data to the insurance market and just more comfort in understanding the technology behind blockchain. So partnerships and relationships go a long way in the insurance industry. Insurance really is vital to growing an industry and business. It helps companies grow. Traditional insurers like you think AIG, Excel, Lloyds of London, Zurich for example, those big name insurers are very well funded and they know how to pay claims. What matters most when it comes to insurance is if they'll pay a claim. So there are a lot of new carriers out there who are advertising that they are focusing on the blockchain space. And maybe they are and maybe they'll be great. But unfortunately we don't have the history to show whether they'll pay claims, which is really what matters. We also don't know how well funded they are, so how many big claims they can actually pay out before they can't pay any more claims. So we work with the traditional insurers who meet certain financial requirements and will step up and who we know will pay claims. And we can all work together, whether it's with us, whether you work with other brokers or carriers directly, to help shape the underwriting process of those experienced insurance markets when it comes to blockchain and digital asset exposure. Believe it or not, the insurance carriers need you as much as you need them. So please take advantage of that and we hope to talk to you all soon. .我很

So what I want to talk about now is how to think about augmented reality as it's developing. And if any of you agree or disagree with the thoughts that I put forward here, I would love to hear your thoughts and have them come talk to me afterwards. But as far as a platform goes, that is what we see on the left here. The platform of augmented reality headsets is hands -free computing. That's really what the platform is. The interface is all the cool stuff we can do with the data that we would visualize, the holograms, et cetera. So I think it's the hands -free computing is what makes the platform so interesting. And then, of course, the interface in the future. This is really what Meta is kind of focused on is how do you make the interface of augmented reality that more naturally connects with your kind of mental state or how you learn, things like that. So we've got a platform right now. The interface is still being developed. So how can you develop things for the community or the enterprise world or the commercial world if really what you have is the platform? You need to think about how to optimize around that. Thanks for coming. So I'm gonna share some experiences with you about this product we did with regional fire departments to see if we could help their sense of orientation using augmented reality. So first of all, fire still has a major impact on our society. We do more and more in prevention, but there is about half a million fires per year in the U.S. with all the human and economic costs that are related to it. So it makes sense to not just work on prevention, but also give firefighters the best tools that we can think of to help them do their work. And one of the most important elements in that is speed at the moment. When an alarm goes in a fire department, they manage to leave within two minutes, just stop whatever they were doing, get in the truck, go on their way. And then these are European numbers, but I assume it's the same here in the U.S. Fire stations are placed in such a way that within eight minutes maximum, they can reach the majority of the population. And then when they arrive on site, obviously the stress is still there, but they take about up to 13 minutes to search, to get out and search, well, let's say a four -room apartment and bring people out of the building. This is very fast and I think it's a great achievement considering, I mean, eight minutes to get anywhere in the town is usually already very fast. But it's always too slow. Unfortunately, once you, when you're in an environment with toxic smoke, you lose consciousness within, let's say, 13 minutes and another four minutes more and they might be too late. So what we're working on in this project is to try to make this last, the last step like of the intervention, make it faster. Because there is a big component which slows down the work of firefighters and it's smoke. Smoke is very problematic because you don't see much. You literally don't see more than a few centimeters in front of you. And it forces them to work with their hands, hands on the wall to navigate with safety lines. They're staying in groups together. And now and then they stop and use a thermal camera to scan because infrared has a nice advantage that it goes through most smoke particles. So you get quite a good view of the environment. So there is already a part of the solution, but it's not hands -free. So we thought we can improve this by using surprise, surprise, augmented reality. We wanted to project a thermal image in the field of view that allows them to move more freely and have a permanent good view of the environment. So we made a proof of concept and it looks like this where you see nothing. You just see smoke. And the thermal imaging really allows you to see people that you didn't see before. It allows them, when they use the fire hose, to spray exactly at the hottest spot of the fire. Because usually, as soon as you open the fire hose, there's just steam and there's nothing you can see anymore. And with if you have thermal imaging, you can see actually where you're pointing with your fire hose, and you can point very nicely. And they can do that nowadays with a handheld thermal camera. But if you have a handheld thermal camera, you cannot hold your fire hose. So it's not a very practical tool. And yeah, we took the thermal image and we projected it on a transparent screen. And obviously, that's not so nice. Handheld cameras often use black and white images for the thermal. You cannot see that on the thermal image. So we worked a lot on making good visualization algorithms that both show very clear contours of the environment, but also still show the temperature. For firefighters, temperature is very important. There's a few risk zones where you want to know what the temperature is. And we did all this with off -the -shelf components. So the proof of concept was based on a pair of Epson glasses and a sensor we could just buy. And then we did lots of tests in realistic conditions. So we used fire simulators for people who've never been there. Those are just concrete raw buildings with a lot of smoke and gas fire generators where you can do very nice realistic tests and show that actually the performance of the firework improves using our system. And then what we found is very important is really talk with the subjects, like really get all the information out, whether they are happy, whether they're not afraid, whether it doesn't block their vision, whether they feel empowered by it, and try to get all the details out about how they experience the system. And all that was very, very positive. So we keep going because this was the proof of concept that we made this convincing video with. As you can see, a GoPro on top, which is not necessary, but it's necessary for filming so we can study later what we're doing, but it's not part of the concept. But this is obviously not usable in firefighting. mean, firefighters use masks, breathing masks, when they go into buildings where they get oxygen because you don't want to breathe the toxic smoke. And so now we're working on integrating that. We hired a little team and we're working on integrating the components and our visualization algorithm into one of these masks. So, well, hopefully in three to six months, we have a prototype that we can demo in more realistic conditions. And in my next talk, I'll tell you about the challenges of making all this hardware robust for firefighting because that's what we're working on now. Thank you very much.

The way we classify use cases is actually we've standardized it. So back in our early days, 2011, 2012, we started counting use cases. And in the six years that I've been doing this, I haven't found any of that kind of fall outside of these buckets. I have found some that are combinations of them. And I believe that the top three are pretty technologically ready, which is inspection and quality assurance, work instructions at kind of a micro level, a very interpersonal interaction with a set of objects for delivering instructions and training using AR to teach a skilled workforce how to do complex things. These are the things that we're doing today at Newport News and things that we're starting to kind of roll out at scale. The middle band, workflow management, that's work instructions at a macro scale. Can a construction supervisor or general foreman or lead general foreman put people to work on the right things? I'd love to tell you a really fun story. It takes about 20 minutes, so I'm going to skip it today. But if you want to hear it, grab me some time and I'll tell you. Okay. Operational situational awareness. To me, this again is using AR as the interface for or edge device for an Internet of Things solution. What's the flow rate in that pipe? What's the electrical state of this cabinet? What paint goes on that bulkhead? It's not an instruction per se. It's awareness and how do you interact with your reality. Okay. And then safety. We care a lot about safety in our business. Can I use AR to make people safer, more situationally aware, see things that aren't there, alert people to things that are happening in their environment? To me, this is the big use case for head mounted. Everything I've talked about to this point, we're deploying with tablets. The last one for us, the most immature technologically speaking is logistics. Okay. Moving people and things around 500 acres of industrial awesomeness, building aircraft carriers and submarines. So what like to do in my remaining time is talk about the mature ones, and I want to show you a new video. Okay. Inspection. This is a fun deployment that we did this year for a submarine that was in our shipyard for her post shakedown availability, the USS John Warner. We're doing a hull inspection with augmented reality. First of its kind, single ship payback from a cost perspective, inspecting the hull using AR. Okay. A real AR deployment for inspection and quality assurance. If you heard me speak in the first session, you heard me talk about that really high value use case. Well, maybe if you missed it, I should refresh it. We did a deployment for inspection where we're looking for temporary structure in a ship that traditionally relies on paper documentation. You know, flipping through page after page after page after drawing to identify structure in your space that was there to support the super lift, but doesn't belong on the ship so we cut it out after the fact. Thirty -six hours of planned inspection work was accomplished in 90 minutes using augmented reality. All right. High impact selections sell it. All right. That's another inspection quality assurance style use case. Work instructions. Okay. One of the things that I'm very cautious with in my estimation of the thousands and thousands of work packages that get deployed into the shipyard every year to build very large complex things, I'd say only about 20 % of them are conducive to AR. The rest of them belong on a VR interface tablet, pin, zoom, rotate. That's all you need. All right. Insert tab A into sloppy. You don't need to augment that. It's overkill. Okay. But if you have that right spatial relevance for a particular use case, AR is huge. Okay. This particular case is in a tank of a ship and we're running cables from point A to point B. Okay. Can I highlight the hangers that they belong in, look at it with a tablet and deploy and install installation trade, electrical trade in this case to install cables more quickly? Okay. These are the places where AR shines in our environment. Last picture I want to talk about, training. Can we do practicals on the job training, do refresher courses with augmented reality in the field? Really, really powerful stuff. Gotten some really great results. But the caution I would give to the AR community is don't try and compete against your VR brothers for training. There's lots of use cases for virtual reality training and if you're trying to compete directly against it, you've already picked the wrong use case.
